Before the Orders of the Day are called, I find myself under the necessity of again alluding to a serious state of affairs that exists in a portion of the Northwest Territories, and if necessary I shall conclude with a motion.
About ten days ago I received a message from the village of Davidson, on the Regina and Prince Albert branch railway, which I placed before the government and the House. That message set forth that the settlers in that locality were entirely unable to obtain seed for their fields this year on account of the breakdown of the railway service. My hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) on that occasion, ten days ago, gave me definite assurance that he would make an attempt to have such steps taken as would ensure to these settlers a supply of seed grain. I stated at that time my apprehension that possibly other localities on the same line of railway were labouring under the same difficulty. I find that my fears in that respect were only too well justified, because I have now received another message from another town on that line-Hanley. That message is as follows :
We are short of provisions, seed grain and farm implements. Situation is serious and immediate relief is prayed for. Can get no information from local officials and desire you to take the matter up in earnest. Reply and give Mr. FIELDING.
us some information that we may know what we have to face.

On behalf of citizens.
I do not need to say to the House that this is a most serious condition of affairs. There are thousands of people who have gone into that section of the country within the past year and who find themselves to-day not only deprived of implements and seed grain, rendering them unable to go on with the seeding operations, but, if we are to believe the words of this despatch, which, I may say, has come from Mr. K. B. Birkeland on behalf of the citizens, they are actually face to face with starvation because they are short of provisions.
Who owns the railway ?

past ; (and as has been the ease every few months for years ;) to have in prospect as at the present time, a famine in seed grain, and a famine in agricultural implements ; to be actually face to face with starvation because of dearth of provisions ; to have as has been the case last winter and during previous winters, actual famine in fuel supply for weeks at a time ; all these things mean that the people were better off before they had a line of railway at all. As mv hon. friend from Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) pointed out the other day, before this line was built from Regina to Prince Albert, the people who lived in the country then were far better off in the matter of transportation than the people are now. The old stage line running from the village of Qu'Appelle to Prince Albert in the earlier days, gave more regular and more secure service, than is given at the present time, or than has been given for many years by this railway company. I have, on previous occasions, alluded in pretty strong language to the transactions which have brought about the results of which I am complaining. and to call these transactions rascally is not putting the matter in too strong language. I would say that the rascality which was perpetrated in the financing of these railways has produced great damage, not only to the people who immediately suffer the lack of railway service, but to the people of the whole Dominion of Canada. It has retarded the development of this immense section of the country for practically a decade ; it has condemned northern Alberta and Saskatchewan and the whole district of Assiniboia north of the Qu'Ap-pelle valley, to the poorest apology for a transportation service that can possibly be described. In the case of Saskatchewan, that unfortunate condition is not yet ended, and will not be ended, I fear, until the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific get into these districts. I venture to say that these two railway transactions have done more to damage the credit of Canada on the money markets of the old country than any other railway transaction that can be mentioned. We have had in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific debate, the suggestion made by our friends of the opposition, that it would be far better policy for the opening of the newer parts of Canada to run railways from the north to the south. For instance, seme of our Conservative friends from the district of Montreal, contend that a lateral railway from the east to the west should not be constructed, but that a railway should be built from Montreal up into the northern part of Quebec
What has that to do with your railway ?

I will tell my hon. friend in a moment. Others have contended that a road built from Toronto up through the northern part of Ontario, would serve the Mr. SCOTT.
interest of the Dominion much better than a lateral road from the east to the west. That is just the policy which our hon. friends opposite pursued when they were in power and the Calgary and Edmonton and the Regina and Prince Albert roads were built in furtherance of that policy. I can tell my hon. friends from Ontario and Quebec, that if they are wise they will never consent to a continuance of any such policy, because we have the unfortunate results of it in the Northwest at the present moment. My hon. friends opposite will not be surprised. I imagine, if I am compelled to allude to one of their colleagues in connection with this enterprise.

I rise to a point of order. The hon. gentleman rose to state a grievance with respect to seed grain and provisions and agricultural implements, and instead of confining himself to the subject, he proposes to wander all over the field and discuss all kind of questions. I submit that the hon. gentleman must confine himself to the question he proposed to discuss when he rose to address this House. I ask your ruling.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Scott) proceeded to point out that certain conditions prevail in that section of the country on account of the deficiency of a certain railway. He went on to show the reasons why the railway was in that condition, and unless he ranges further, I think he is fairly within the mark when he goes on to show that certain conditions now prevail in the Northwest to prevent the people from receiving their farm implements and seed grain. I think the hon. member (Mr. Scott) is reasonably within his right in the discussion of the question before the House.
What do you mean by 'reasonably ' ?

I was just remarking when my hon. friend from Peel raised the point of order, that I think my hon. friends will not be surprised if I am obliged to allude to the name of one of their colleagues, the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier), in connection with these transactions. I might confide to you Mr. Speaker-
I again rise to a point of order. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Scott) persists in calling me the member for Peel.

I beg my hon. friend's pardon ; I intended to refer to him as the member for Halton. I am obliged to confide to you Mr. Speaker, that I am not a bit surprised to find some of the members on the other side of the House objecting to my proceeding to deal with these transactions, because it obliges me to allude to the name of their colleague, the junior member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier). I may say that I would very much prefer to have that hon. gentleman here-

Better wait until he comes.
Mr. SCOTT-when I am using the language I am obliged to use. [DOT]

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I beg to call the attention of the hon. member (Mr. Scott) to the fact, that there is a rule which says : that if any hon. gentleman wishes to bring up a question he usually gives notice to the hon. member to whom he is going to refer, and if that hon. gentleman is not in his seat it is always better and wiser to say nothing about it until he is present. That is the spirit of the rule.

Well, Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Osier) is very often not in his seat. I will take this opportunity to ask my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, if he brought to his lieutenant's attention a matter of information which I quoted here just a week ago to-day and which I asked him at that time to be good enough to bring to the attention of his lieutenant from West Toronto, because I considered that the matter which was discussed at that time was one concerning which that gentleman should attempt to make some explanation. I wish therefore to ask the hon. the leader of the opposition, whether he did call to the attention of the member for West Toronto the information concerning the sale of lands by the Calgary and Edmonton Land Company, reported to have taken place last year.
If the hon. member (Mr. Scott) wishes to send any message to the hon. member for West Toronto, he had better do it directly. I do not propose to be the bearer of bis messages.

I am somewhat surprised at the curt answer given by my hon. friend the pleader of the opposition, for the reason especially that on many occasions since the commencement of this session, the hon. leader of the opposition has displayed what I described a week ago. as a very worthy solicitude for the reputation of the hon. member for West Toronto. As he apparently has failed to meet the request which I made a week ago. I shall have to
attempt on this occasion to make my remarks pointed enough, so that the hon. gentleman will in some manner have his attention called to the matter ; because the people in Northern Alberta, Saskatchewan and Northern Assiniboia, as well as the members of this House, have some right to a further explanation, which that hon. gentleman can give, in reference to these transactions which have resulted so disastrously to large sections of the people of this country. I may say that I have good authority for looking to the hon. junior member for West Toronto for an explanation with regard to any matter in connection with the Qu'Ap-pelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway. About two years ago I was a member of a delegation at Regina which called upon the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, Sir Thomas Shaugh-nessy, who was accompanied by one of the directors of his company, who happened to be the junior member for West Toronto. The delegation brought to the attention of Sir Thomas Shaughnessy certain matters in connection with the operation of this road , running from Regina to Prince Albert, and he referred the delegation to his friend, Mr. E. B. Osier, the junior member for West Toronto, and told them that they would be obliged to look to him for any information or any satisfaction of their claim with regard to that railway, because he was-I think the words of Sir Thomas Shaughnessy were-the owner of the road ; at all events, he gave to it be understood that he was the controller of the road. Now, as everybody in the House knows, that hon. gentleman has of late constituted himself a very severe critic of railway financing. A few days ago in this House, in discussing this matter he stated :
Let us not fake and fool people into investing in wildcat securities

Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman who is addressing the House has already on three occasions referred to the debate on the Grand Trunk Pacific. Unless we are going to have that all over again in this debate, the hon. gentleman should be called to order.
Especially I think he should not have attacked the hon. member for West Toronto in his absence. This is the second or third time that he has done it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman was referring to a previous debate. he knows that he is out of order. Of course, he can refer in a general way in illustration, but he cannot quote or use or combat an argument that has been used in a previous debate. He understands that thoroughly.

Yes, Mr. Speaker, I do understand that it is contrary to the rules to quote from a previous debate; but I

would submit that if any bon. member is going to be prohibited from referring to subjects which have been dealt with in previous debates, the business of this House would not go on in the smooth manner in which it is usually conducted. It is a common occurrence for members to make reference to subjects which have been dealt with in previous debates. I do not propose to quote from a previous debate ; and if I am out of order, I shall be obliged to make no references at all. What I was going to do, when I was called to order, was to refer to the further criticism made by the hoii. junior member for West Toronto, against my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton). I am not going to quote his words, but if I recollect aright, he stated that the speech made by the hon. Minister of the Interior in this House would do, or had done, more to discredit Canadian securities and Canadian enterprise in the old country than anything else that had transpired. If that hon. gentleman were here-and I am sorry that he is not-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member must remember that violating the rule with regard to a previous debate does not consist simply in the reading of a quotation from it, but in assuming an argu-' ment and basing another argument thereon. Otherwise rre could discuss the entire question without any quotations at all. A member cannot take up an argument used in a previous debate, and base an argument upon that to be used in a succeeding debate without violating the rule.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Certainly.

Thank you. The hon. gentleman rose in his seat on the 3rd of September, 1903. on a question of privilege, and made not only an explanation, but an absolute and direct denial of practically everything I said. He declared that he was not a promoter or charter holder in either the Calgary and Edmonton, or the Qu'Ap-pelle Long Lake and Saskatchewan, that he had not made one dollar of profit out of them, that no on? had made anything because the whole of the government subvention of land and money had to be

pledged, together with the bonds, to raise the money required, and that the difference between the money obtained and the cost of the roads lnvi to be left in the hands of the bankers as a guarantee of the interest. The House may be interested if I read a little newspaper paragraph which appeared in the Winnipeg ' Telegram ' of Tuesday, 3rd of May 1904. The paragraph is the following :
Last year, when Mr. Scott brought this subject up, he charged that the transaction had involved something of a swindle

That is not exactly correct. I do not think that I charged anything in the nature of a swindle against my hon. friend from West Toronto, but let it pass.
Mr. Osier who w'as engaged in financing this enterprise, took issue with him and made an explanation which made Mr. Scott look a little small. He was compelled to apologize for some of the expressions he used at the time. He has evidently not had enough of it, and is now coming back for more. Mr. Osier was not present when the subject was brought up to-day but will no doubt be heard from in due time.
I sincerely trust that the hon. gentleman will be heard from, in due time, from his place in this House in further explanation of this matter. It is perfectly true that, in the face of the absolute and direct denial of the statements which I made last year, which the hon. the junior member for Toronto saw fit to make from his place in this House, I did deem it my duty to retract certain of the statements which on a previous day I had made in this House. The following is one of the assertions which the hon. gentleman made at that time and which will be found on page 10499 of the revised ' Hansard ' of last year :
I do not know why they should go out of their way to make statements, which one can hardly believe they didn't know to be absolutely false. I had nothing to do with the chartering of these roads.
By the rules of the House I was obliged to accept that statement, and therefore retracted the charge I had made that the hon. gentleman had something to do with the promotion and chartering of these roads. But to my surprise, on turning up the statutes, I found that in chapter 84 of the statutes of 1S90, one of the names appearing in the list of chartered members of the Calgary and Edmonton Railway Company, is that of Edmund B. Osier. That is the fact which supports my conclusion that the hon. gentleman, who now represents West Toronto, was a promoter and charter holder in that company. The hon. gentleman said again on page 10503 :
I was not a promoter of either the Calgary and Edmonton or the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway. I deny it absolutely.
But. Mr. Speaker, as I have just pointed out, the hon. gentleman's name appears in chapter 84 of the Statutes of 1890, among those who made application to this parliament to be organized as a company for the construction of the Calgary and Edmonton Railway. At page 10498, I find the hon. gentleman reported as having said, referring to the Calgary and Edmonton :
A new charter was obtained by some people.
There had been previously a charter in existence covering the same territory :
A new charter was obtained by some people -I was not one of them-with a grant of 6,400 acres per mile and $80,000 per year for twenty years in lieu of government service.
And on page 10,497, he used these words with reference to the financing of the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway company .
I succeeded in raising the money by the sale of the land grant and sale of the bonds.
At page 10489, referring to the Calgary and Edmonton, he said :
The road was financed in precisely the same manner as I have described in connection with the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway. $5,000,000 was raised by the sale of the land and of the bonds.
Again at page 10502, he said :
I make the statement that the lands were spjd at the time ; but they were sold with the bonds in both cases, and the whole of the money that was raised from the sale of lands and bonds went into the roads and paid interest on the roads.
On page 10499 he said :
Every dollar that went into the construction of the roads was paid in cash.
Now, the fact is cited against me that last year I retracted and apologized to the hon. gentleman. What else could any one in my position have done in face of these direct statements ? What interpretation could any one place upon the distinct and absolute denial made by the , hon. friend from his place in the House? What interpretation was placed upon his language by other hon. members? I find that the right hon. the Prime Minister said he understood from Mr. Osier's words that Mr. Osier ' was not one of the promoters and that not one dollar of that money-had gone into his pockets.' The hon. gentleman's colleague from Toronto (Mr. Clarke) thus gave his interpretation of the" hon. gentleman's language :
Mr. Osier declared that in making these financial arrangements and in disposing of the bonds necessary for building the roads, the land grant:? were sold at the same time, and every dollar ihus raised was put into the roads 'or set apart foi interest.



The hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Ingram) also understood Mr. Osier's language to mean :
The 'non. member for West Toronto has stated here to-day, on his honour as a gentleman, that he was not one of the promoters, but simply an agent.
Yet, when I turn up the statutes, I find his name in the list of charter holders in this railway company. These are the statements and the circumstances. I have shown some of the facts with regard to which the Winnipeg ' Telegram ' makes the statement that Mr. Osier was able to make a reply which made the hon. member for West Assiniboda look small. Well, 1 have some further information besides what I bad last year. I have now the prospectus that was issued by this railway company in London in 1889. In quoting the extract, I would ask the House to remember the statement made by the hon. member for West Toronto, that he was obliged to pledge the lands with the bonds in order to raise the money which he secured for the building of these roads :
The total issue will be secured by a first mortgage in trust upon the railway from Regina to Prince Albert, excluding the land grant, and the proceeds are sufficient for, and will be applied towards, the construction of the line.
I should think that would be sufficient- almost twice as much as they put into the roads.
$80,000 a year for twenty years (annual subsidy) will be paid over direct to trustees for the bondholders.
That is the government subvention in cash.
The company are further entitled to a grant of about 1,400,000 acres of selected lands ; a sale of a considerable portion has just been concluded, the proceeds of which will be paid to the agents of the loan, and will be sufficient to provide the balance of the interest on the above bonds until 1st February, 1896. On 1st February, 1896, the Canadian Pacific Railway will, on giving six months' notice have power of calling in and paying off the above bonds at 110.
Alluding to the circumstances 1 have already mentioned, the hon. member's opinion of what would discredit Canadian securities on the London money market, let me read an extract also from a letter of one of the bondholders of this company, one of the men who put up the money to carry out this undertaking. Let us see what this investor thinks about the methods of finance of the hon. member for West Toronto. This letter is written from England and it says in part:
The land grant was not mortgaged to the bondholders. Consequently, I suppose, the * company ' whose issued capital is $210,000, had the right to sell the land, (except one-third of it kept in hand by the government, I can't quite see why) and they did so.
What is his name 7

I am sorry, but I have not this gentleman's permission to give his name, but if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hag-gart) is anxious to have it, I think I may be able to obtain permission, in which case, I will give it to him privately. Now, this hon. gentleman from West Toronto is a great stickler for parliamentary ethics. On the whole, he is a very great man. Common, ordinary representatives from the Northwest Territories are entirely beneath his notice. He said so himself. He told the House last session that the statement I made here with regard to his connection with these roads was not worthy of his attention. And he told us that it was because of a reference made by a newspaper in the country that he thought it worth while to make any representations on the subject last year. We in the Northwest are good enough to pay dividends on the hon.

gentleman's roads. We; also have still the right to breathe the air, which is about the only thing in the Northwest that hon. gentlemen opposite, when they were in power, did not give these corporations a monopoly of. And we have a right to occupy seats in this House, if we can get here over the strength of the hon. gentleman's money. But, otherwise, we livfe only by the hon. gentleman's gracious permission, and we remain entirely beneath his notice. He is a very self-sacrificing gentleman. He has told us that himself also. He went to a great deal of trouble to build these roads for us-so he confided to us last year-and did it entirely without profit to himself. He has given us to understand also that his extreme opposition to the Grand Trunk Pacific is entirely against his own personal interest. I quote in this instance his own words. He says that if the Grand Trunk Pacific scheme is carried out, it will be of enormous benefit to the Canadian Pacific Railway of which he is a director and a shareholder and a member, as the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Cowan) told us of the inner board or cabinet. It is a peculiar fact that every representative of the Canadian Pacific Railway whom we have heard speak takes the same view of the Grand Trunk Pacific as the hon. member for West Toronto. That hon. gentleman is not quite fair to his colleagues of the Canadian Pacific Railway board when he seeks to claim a monopoly of patriotism of that directorate with regard to the Grand Trunk Pacific proposition; We have heard Sir William Van Horne on that subject and Sir Thomas Shaughnessy also. I suppose that the speech that Sir Thomas Shaughnessy delivered in Toronto some time ago was intended wholly to improve the prospects of the Grand Trunk Pacific. And we have been told also-I have not looked up the facts myself-that one of the directors of the Grand Trunk Pacific in London, Mr. Thos. Skinner, is editor of the ' Canadian Gazette.'
If his attitude, as exploited in the pages of the ' Canadian Gazette,' indicates approval of the Grand Trunk Pacific proposition it is a matter of very great surprise to those who have read his articles. Sir Sand-ford Fleming is a director of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and is sometimes quoted in approval of the Grand Trunk Pacific, but even his statement, if you examine it carefully, means that he simply approves of the building of a road entirely north of Lake j Winnipeg, of Manitoba and of the whole organized Territories, so far north indeed that it shall not cause any competition or affect in any way either by way of benefit or damage to the Canadian Pacific Railway. Thus I think that the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) is not quite fair to his colleagues on the Canadian Pacific Railway board when he seeks to convince this House 8Si
that the other gentlemen connected with that company favour the Grand Trunk Pacific because it is going to be an enormous benefit to them. The hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) as I have explained, went to England with $12,000,000 worth of good Canadian securities in his pocket to float two schemes which demanded really only $6,000,000, and he could only get the $6,000,000 by guaranteeing additional securities in the shape of bonds worth $10,000,000. And he comes here and asks us to believe that in order to be able to bring back the $6,000,000 he was compelled to pledge the $12,000,000 worth of cash and lands, the securities which he took over with him, also create further $10,000,000 in bonds securities, and in addition to that he has told us that he had to leave some $3,000,000 of the cash in the hands of bankers in England as a guarantee of six years' interest on the bonds which yielded $9,263,653.
Before I proceed further you will perhaps permit me to read to the House an opinion from outside parties upon these transactions. I have here a very brief letter from a gentleman at Pincher Creek which came to me shortly after the debate last year. It is dated September 5, 1903, and is as follows :	,
I thank you with all my heart for showing up so boldly and clearly the infamous boodling connected with the Calgary and Edmonton and other roads in the past. We in Pincher Creek, away from the Calgary and Edmonton line al-togther, have suffered for years from this robbery of our lands and are suffering now. The towns of Macleod and Edmonton suffered by the villainous attempt to make them move by not running the Calgar^ and Edmonton line into them.
Cannot steps be taken

I would ask the right hon. the leader of the government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) to give attention to this paragraph :
-to make these boodlers disgorge their ill-gotten gains ? There have been impeachments for similar robbery of public money before now. It would have a most wholesome effect.
Would the hon. gentleman be good enough to give us the name of the writer ?

In this case as in the other I have not the writer's permission to give his name, but I will probably be able to secure it.
This other letter is from a gentleman who is algo financially interested, through old country connections, with the bonds of the Prince Albert branch, and he says :
One thing I can not understand, and that is how Osier makes out that it took $1,500,000 to pay interest on the bonds of the company for 6 years, and why if he had raised the money it was not deposited in the Dominion Savings Bank instead of adding to the private hoards of Morton, Rose & Co. ; it is quite inconceivable too how he can explain the way in which the entire handling of these lands has been

done by his firm up to last year, if he had nothing to do with it, and lands had been already sold ; I think he is himself the president of the Qu'Appelle road and so is doubly liable to the bondholders.
Reference is then made to a supplement to my own speech which included 'a letter from Mr. Hugh Sutherland, which this gentleman says he had never seen before, and which he says is very interesting. He then proceeds :
I should think a debate like that, with the gloves off, would make such deals very nearly impossible in the future, but that does not help the widows and orphans who have been victimized by this past deal.
Will the hon. gentleman tell us who used that language ?
This gentleman is a very respectable resident of the Northwest Territories, whose name I have not the privilege of communicating to the House.
Then don't read the letter.

My hon. friend will permit me to use my own discretion in that regard. The gentleman proceeds :
I should very much like to hear the real ' inwards ' of the Osler-Hammond deal with Morton Rose ; McCreary exactly hit the nail when he said that the bonds were taken up on the strength of the assertion that the bonds would in all probability be taken up by the Canadian Pacific Railway at 110 ; the Canadian Pacific Railway give no separate accounts of the profits of their lease in their annual report and the report of the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake is very silent about facts and figures, and is very hard to get even by the bondholders.

Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Scott) wish us to understand that the writers of these three letters have asked him to read these letters in the House, and at the same time refuse to tell us who the writers are ?
My hon. friend (Mr. Lancaster) quite misunderstands me, I have not stated that the writers asked me to read the letters.
And at the same time to refuse to say who the authors were.

I would repeat to my hon. friend that I have not stated that the writers asked me to read the letters in the House. The last two of these letters which I have read were written to me ; the one from the old country bondholder was sent to another gentleman in the Northwest Territories. not to myself, but it has been put in my hands. I have not at the present time the permission of the writers to give their names to the House, but if my hon. friend is anxious I have not the slightest doubt that- in due course I can obtain that permission.
Has he the permission of these gentlemen to use that language in this House and at the same time to refuse to give their names ?
I have no intention of permitting myself to be cross-examined on this occasion.
We want to know who used that language.

I have read the letters ; they were actually written by people who knew what they were writing about, and I state that on my responsibility as a member. It is my privilege to decide whether I shall divulge the names.
Does the hon. gentleman state that they were written to be read in this House ?
I have distinctly stated twice that I did not say so, but I have given the House the advantage of the contents of the letters.
It would be a great advantage to know who wrote them.

I have already gone over the ground that the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) asserted flatly that he was not a promoter or charter holder, and I have also referred at some length to the statement that the land was pledged in both cases with the bonds. I have in the House the actual mortgage deed with regard to the Calgary and Edmonton road, but I will save time by reading from it only the clause which refers to the matter in question.
What evidence has the gentleman given that the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Osier) is a promoter ?
We will get the Act.
It is in the statutes of 1890.
Then an incorporator in a railway charter is necessarily a promoter ?

If my hon. friend will permit me I will return to the statement that was made by the hon. member for West Toronto who stated that:
I had nothing to do with the chartering of these roads. ... I was not a promoter of either. I deny it absolutely. A new charter was obtained by some people-I was not one of them.	[DOT]
This in face of the fact that the hon. gentleman's name appears amongst the list of charter holders.
The new charter? .

The new charter. The list will be found in chapter 84 of the statutes of 1890. Now, in regard to his claim that the land had to be pledged as security for

the bonds it is interesting to look up the mortgage deed and this is a reference to one of the clauses :
It is stated in such mortgage deed and in the bond certificates, that the bonds are secured by conveyance, by way of mortgage, to the trustees of the company's railway, with its revenues, &e., including an annual subsidy of $80,000.	' it being, however, expressly understood that the subsidy or land grant from the government, excepting as it forms an actual part of the company's line, shall be excepted from the operation of the said mortgage and shall form no part of the security for the payment of the said bonds or the interest thereon.'
That is a provision contained in the clause of the mortgage deed in reference to the Calgary and Edmonton Railway. In the statute respecting the Qu'Appelle Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway there is a subclause numbered (e) of section 1 :
In subclause (e) of section 1 of an agreement between the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Company and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, confirmed by chapter 82, 53 Victoria, it is recited that the former company ' shall not issue any bonds secured, directly or indirectly, on its land subsidies or any portion of such land subsidies, except so much of those lands, if any, as shall be actually taken for the line of railway and stations .'
' By subclause (c) of section 3 of the aforesaid agreement, it is recited that ' it is understood and declared that the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Company may transfer one-half of the land subsidy from the Dominion government, from time to time, as it shall be earned, to any person or persons, as it may deem proper.'
This is apparently a provision which the hon. member for West Toronto and his associates took good advantage of. Then, his statement was that to guarantee six years' interest on the bonds the difference of 53,000,490 between the proceeds of the bonds and the cost of the road had to be left in the banker's hands. That statement will bear a little investigation. Surely this very able financier did not contract to pay interest on the money that he left in the hands of the bankers. Surely the three million dollars which he said he left in the hands [DOT]of the bankers attended to its own interest and no payment of interest there would be required. The road cost $6,283,162. Six per cent interest and that was the rate for six years would make $2,261,,934. But, we have to keep in mind the -fact that the bondholders were given a cash pledge from the government amounting to $80,000 per year on each road, or $160,000 per year on the two roads. In six years that would amount to $960,000, leaving a difference required to be provided to meet the total interest charges during these six years of $1,301,934, apart altogether from the portion of the land grant, which, as it appears by the prospectus of the Prince Albert Company, was sold and the proceeds handed over as a part of the amount to be
used in payment of the six years' interest. Perhaps the hon. member for South Lanark will be good enough, as the hon. leader of the opposition has declined to do it, to bring this matter to the attention of his hon. friend from West Toronto and ask him to repeat, if he dares repeat, the statement he made last year that he was obliged to pledge the whole of the land together with the bonds to raise the money for the building of these roads, that he was obliged to leave $3,000,490 with the bankers to meet the interest, which, even without any proceeds from the sale of land, required as I have shown, only a matter of $1,301,934. I will send over to the hon. member for South Lanark now the statutes of 1890. containing chapter 84, which includes his friend's name. That hon. gentleman who so far is not able or does not dare to repeat the assertions he made last year will perhaps be good enough to come to his place in this House and explain what became of this balance of $1,698,447. The House and the people of this country are interested in knowing and particularly the people who ought to be served and who are not served by the railways which were the result of this transaction are interested in knowing. Let us remember that the greater portion of the lands remain still to be accounted for entirely apart from the amount of $1,698,447. I will say to my hon. friends opposite that the lands were not pledged with the bonds and that the whole of the lands were not sold at the time the bonds were sold, and I will give to the House before I am through the actual disposition from the Department of the Interior of the lands, the actual people who obtained the patents of the lands which were granted in aid of the construction of these roads. I will tell the hon. member for South Lanark who may be good enough to bring it to the attention of his hon. friend from West Toronto, that, owing to the horn-swoggling with about one and a half million dollars and the hornswoggling also with the land grants voted by this parliament to these companies, brought about by selling at a very low price to subsidiary land companies, which the hon. member for West Toronto organized, with which he has been connected ever since, being a director of one of them. I believe, lands which he told us he was obliged to pledge to the bondholders, the people of the west have been subjected to the disabilities of which we complain today. If the matter of $500,000 that the Calgary and Edmonton Land Company were able to get out of the 130,000 acres of land which they sold last year had been devoted to the betterment of these roads the people of the Saskatchewan district would not have been obliged to send the telegrams which my hon. friend from Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) and myself have been called upon to read on more than one occasion, because, otherwise, these roads would not

have been in the deplorable shape in which they are found to-day. I have here a statement from the Department of the Interior in regard to the patenting of these lands. It is as follows :

At the end of thirteen years the Prince Albert Railway Company were still in a position to deal with a new company, the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company, composed of American land dealers, and they assigned to them last year 840,229 acres, making a total of 1,126,230 acres, which was the total area earned by the Prince Albert Company. The hon. gentleman from West Toronto (Mr. Osier) took vigorous exception to a phrase quoted by the right hon. Prime Minister respecting, if I recollect aright, 'monied and ownied men,' the Prime Minister explaining that the latter term meant landed proprietors or landlords. The hon. gentleman from West Toronto took the exception that there were no landed proprietors in this country, but it appears to me that a gentleman who was permitted to exploit-if that is the proper term-who was permitted to manipulate, or at all events in some manner to horn-swoggle with three and a half million acres of the good land of the Northwest Territories, should not take such an objection, for if there is a landed proprietor any where in the world, it seems to me that the hon. gen-Mr. SCOTT.
tleman might be put within that class. My hon. friends of the opposition have been professing for some time to have a very keen interest in the transportation question in the Northwest Territories. They take a very minute interest in the Grand Trunk Pacific question. Let me say to them that there are tens of thousands of people who occupy a very large section of the Northwest Territories, and whose main interest in the Grand Trunk Pacific proposition has resulted from these indefensible transactions which I have been describing this afternoon. If any of my hon. friends opposite are good enough to get up and make any reference to this matter with which I have been detaining the House for the last hour and a quarter-
We are not anxious to waste the time of the House ; we want to do business.

I have no doubt they will take me to task, as they did last year, for presuming, as they call it, to waste the time of the House in dealing with such a subject. In my opinion, a subject which has to do with about three and a half millions acres of land of the Northwest Territories, a subject that has to do with the resources of this country to the extent of more than $9,000,000, a subject which has to do with 550 miles of railway, a subject that has to do with a vital interest-an interest so vital that there are many hundreds of people to-day north of the Qu'Appelle valley and south of the south branch of the Saskatchewan river actually face to face with starvation ; in my opinion, I need not apologize for bringing such a question before the parliament of Canada. Mr. Speaker, my colleagues from the Northwest Territories and myself are going to continue to ventilate this subject until a proper and effective remedy is found by the parliament of this country for the conditions which are the result of these transactions. Hon. gentlemen opposite are to-day very severe critics of our railway transactions, but the kind of transactions which I have pointed out are those for which they are themselves responsible. They have been asking the Prime Minister day after day, since the commencement of the session: Why, if the people of Canada are going to contribute so much for the Grand Trunk Pacific and the company itself so little, why does not the country own the whole concern? We may very well ask in regard to these two railroads I have referred to, why, if the people of Canada contributed the whole thing- not only the whole thing, but twice as much in resources as was needed to construct the roads ; why, if the country contributed an amount equal to $22,000 per mile, while the roads themselves, by the records of the Railways and Canals Department, only amounted to a matter of $11,000 per mile ; why, if the country in this case contributed, not only the whole thing, but twice the whole thing, we may ask, did it come that the govern-
2T81

ment didn't retain possessioin of the road for the people of Canada rather than hand it over to a corporation ?
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that both are bad ?
I do not quite understand.
Do I understand from the hon. gentleman's argument that both systems are bad-two wrongs do not make a right ?
The case I am speaking about this afternoon is radically bad.
And the other is only relatively bad ?

I know that the people are complaining with good reason about this case of which I am speaking. In my opinion, it is a matter of very little moment who is. the owner of a railway if the people are ensured fair rates and a reasonable service on that railway. Notwithstanding that private corporations may own these roads, if the people had fair rates upon them and were able to get a reasonable service, in fact any service at all, I would not have to complain in this House to-day. I read at the opening of my remarks a telegram in which the people of that country complain that they are faced with starvation.

Who is the telegram from ?
Mr. -SCOTT. It is from Mr. K. B. Birke-land, on behalf of the citizens of the town of Hanley. It is but the duplicate of another telegram which I read in the House ten days ago. The people along that whole line of railway are obliged to complain. As I pointed out when the hon. gentleman was not in the House, they are new settlers in these districts, this is their first seeding season, and they are obliged to Import their grain.
Mr. B'LAIN. Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that this condition of things has been going on for some time in that district ?

There has not before been such a serious state of affairs as we have to complain about at present, but the interruptions in railway traffic in that country have been continuing for many years past. They have been a matter of common occurrence. The hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) has had, on half a dozen occasions, been obliged to complain here of the interruptions in the railway mail service on account of the inefficiency of this railway company, and these interruptions sometimes lasted a week, sometimes two weeks, and sometimes perhaps for a month. It must be patent to everybody that if the. resources of this country, voted to these railway corporations, had been used in behalf of the roads, we
would not now have to complain of these conditions. It is because the resources which were voted to the railroads never went to the benefit of the roads that we have to complain. The hon. gentleman who now represents West Toronto sold bonds on the money market of the old country sufficient, not only sufficient to build the road, but sufficient to give him an amount of cash to leave in the hands of bankers for six years' interest, and the land grants have been used for the benefit of other people ; used for purposes which never allowed them to reach the railway at all. As I have already stated, there was half a million dollars which the Calgary and Edmonton Company was able to get out of 130,000 acres of land last year, and which, if it had gone into betterments on the road, the conditions we have to complain of to-day would not exist. I repeat, in conclusion, that I very much regret that the hon. gentleman from West Toronto (Mr. Osier) is not in his seat. I know that I may be reproached because I discussed this matter again in his absence, but I am bound to say that the people of that country cannot subordinate their interests entirely to the convenience of the hon. gentleman from West Toronto (Mr. Osier). I explained that this matter was brought up ten days ago when I pointedly asked the leader of the opposition to draw . the attention of his absent friend to the subject, and I expected that the very first day that gentleman (Mr. Osier) came back to the House he would attempt to give some explanation. I took good care to be in the House on the calling of the Orders every day since, but the hon. gentleman (Mr. Osier) has not seen fit to give any word of explanation.
Do you complain that there is a defective service, or that there is no railway service at all ?

Practically none at the present time. ' The bridge over the South Saskatchewan is washed away, the Qu'-Appelle valley is flooded, and there is a practical tie-up of the railway service. This has existed not only for the past week, and even the past month, but, as my hon. friend from Saskatchewan will tell the House, ever since January. He has received telegrams from Kosthern and Prince Albert, which state that consignments of freight from Winnipeg or farther east have been on the road since January and have not yet arrived. What led me to refer to this matter again to-day was the concluding sentence of the telegram that was sent to me, which said :
Reply and give us some information, that we may know what we have to face.
If the people have to face starvation, they want to know it, so, if it is necessary, they will have to take the last means available, and endeavour to get out on their feet.
Might I ask the hon. member if he presented this telegram to the Minister of Railways or made any effort to get the people out of their trouble ?

On the last occasion on which the matter was up, the Minister of Railways was here, and he stated that he intended to inquire into it ; but since that time I have not heard whether he has proceeded any length with his inquiry. Since that time we have received further telegrams, with further and more grievous complaints on the part of the people ; and, although the hon. member for West Toronto is not in his seat, I consider that I am well justified by the facts and the conditions in laying this matter as fully as possible and with as much force as I can command. before the people, the members of this House and the government.

Mr. Speaker, I ask you to direct that these letters which the hon. gentleman has read be laid on the table of the House. I am aware that he has stated that he cannot give the names of the writers, and that wihat I am asking, involves the knowledge by the members of this House that the hon. gentleman has not the permission of the writers to give their names. The hon. gentleman and the writers of the letters may have their rights, but the members of this House have their rights also ; and the veracity, I may say the honour, of an hon. member who is not present is impugned by the alleged evidence contained in these letters. The hon. member for West Toronto has made a statement of facts, and the hon. member for West Assiniboia, not contented with that statement, undertakes to contradict it by certain letters, which, as they stand now, are anonymous. I think that fact takes the letters out of the rule, under which the hon. gentleman could claim them to be private. He should have considered that before he set up the letters against the statement of an hon. gentleman who holds a seat, and holds it very worthily, in this House. The question now, is not only a question of the rights of the writers of these letters and of the hon. member for Western Assiniboia ; but it is a question of the rights of the members of this House to consider the evidence which the hon. gentleman sees fit to put before the House an which to impugn the veracity of the hon. member for West Toronto. Under these circumstances, I would ask you. Mr. Speak-ei, to rule that these letters be laid on the table of this House.
Mr;. SCOTT. I twould ask the hon. member for South Lanark, (Mr. Haggart), to whom I sent the statute a little while ago, to place that on the table. That is a public document, and might very well be placed on the table, as it has a very Mr. SCOTT.
important bearing on this matter. With regard to the letters, I have merely to repeat that I have not permission to place them on the table or to make the names of the writers public at the present time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Do I understand my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) to raise this point as a point of order ?
Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If it is a point of order,. I submit that it is not well taken. If a minister of the Crown reads a state document, it is his duty to place that on the table ; but if a private member reads a letter from any person, I know of no rule which compels him- to place it on the table Cf the House.

I know the rule of the House perfectly well. The hon. member for West Assiniboia made a statement some tjme ago. The hon. member for West Toronto contradicted that statement. The hon. member for West Assiniboia, in the absence of the hon. member for West Toronto, reads a lot of private letters contradicting the statement of the hon. member for West Toronto. According to the rules of the House, the hon. member for West Assiniboia, has no right to read those letters, even though' they may be perfectly true and a justification of his course. It is against the rules of the House for these letters to be read contradicting the statement of the hon. member for West Toronto.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Then hon. gentlemen opposite should have objected when my hon. friend was reading them.

They did object at the time. The letters having been read by the hon. gentleman, are no longer private communications. They are letters attacking the honour of a member of this House, who has given a distinct denial of the statement of the hon. member for West Assiniboia ; yet that hon. member, knowing the rule of the House, knowing that he has no right to read a private letter contradicting the statement of the hon. member for West Toronto, gets up and reads the letter, and then refuses to give the name of the writer. I did not suppose such a case as this has ever occurred before. It never could have occurred in the House of Commons of England, because the Speaker *would have at once stopped it. But the hon. member for West Assiniboia, having once read these letters, I think that it is your duty, Mr. Speaker, to direct that he shall place them upon the table of the House.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
May I say a word on the point of order ? As I understand it, it is as to whether a member of the House, having read a letter addressed to himself or to somebody else, without objection been

raised to his doing so by any member of the House, can be compelled to lay the letter on the table. If hon. gentlemen opposite assert that as a principle, let them cite' their authority. I venture to say that they will not be able to cite any authority whatever. If my hon. friend from West Assiniboia, trespassed on the rule of the House in reading a communication which reflected on a member of this House, that point should have been raised and argued at the time he proposed to read the letter. The only rule there is with regard to compelling a document to be placed on the table of the House, is the well known rule that when any member of the government in debate refers to an official document, the official document must be laid on the table ; but I venture to say that my hon. friend will not be able to cite a case of a member being required to place on the table a private letter from which he has read in the course of his speech, when objection was not taken to his reading it at the time.
Surely my hon. friend remembers that when the hon. member for West Assiniboia was reading the letters I objected to his reading them unless he pave the names of llie writers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If there is anything in the objection as to the hon. members right to read the letters, the giving or not of the names, would make no difference.
Still, the objection was taken.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Asking for the names is not taking an objection to the reading of the documents. If the hon gentleman had no right to read the documents-as to which I express no opinion-he could not put himself in order by giving the names. The objection was not taken to the reading of the letters.
It was taken.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend says he did not object, but only asked for the names. The giving of the names would not make the matter better or worse, so far as the point of order is concerned. The only point now is whether the hon. gentleman is bound to lay the letters on the table.
The hon. minister is confusing the question of waiving an objection and not taking one. I took the objection but was willing to waive it if the hon. gentleman would give us the name.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
What I desire to point out is this. The giving of the names would not make any difference whatever. If the hon. gentleman on the other side-I have forgotten who it was-desired to prevent the reading of the letters, either with the names or without the names, his duty was to submit his objection to you, Mr. Speaker, and ask your ruling. If he could have made
good his point, he would have prevented the reading of the letters. But not having raised that point, the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) is perfectly justified in saying that he read such portions of the documents as he saw fit, that the documents were not public but private documents, and he could not be 'ordered to produce them.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There are two rules which apply to public documents-one of which is applicable to ministers of the Crown and the other to private members. When a minister of the Crown reads a public document, he is bound to place it upon the table if asked so to do. A private member, however, can read from either a private or a public document-according to the rules in England and in the Canadian House- and is not bound to place it on the table, even if requested. If an hon. member reads anything which is a criticism upon what has been said in the House that session and the point of order is raised at the time, he would be ruled out of order. But if he is reading a criticism upon something which was said at a previous session of parliament, he is perfectly in order. The hon. gentleman, when asked to give the name affixed to a letter which he has read, is not bound to do so. The giving of it or not is a matter entirely within his own discretion.

In view of your ruling, Sir, which of course the House will agree to, I have only to say to the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) that as his statements are founded upon what are practically anonymous letters read by him. since he refuses to give the names of the writers, I consider the matter of not sufficient importance to bring to the notice of the hon. member for West Toronto and withdraw my promise to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The question of supplying seed grain to the settlers in the town or village of Davidson upon this line of railway was brought to the attention of the House and the government some days ago. I then said-in reply I think to my hon. friend from West Assiniboia-that I would take steps to see that whatever was necessary would be done in order that these people might have this grain transported to the station from which they could procure it. I immediately did take steps to see that the matter was attended to and on Saturday last my department was advised by our immigration commissioner at Winnipeg that the people of Davidson were supplied with everything required. Anticipating further trouble, instructions were sent to the superintendent of immigration, Mr. W. D. Scott, at Winnipeg, and he went to Regina, and I believe reached that city this morning. I telegraphed him the substance of the complaint from tfhe settlement at Hanley, and asked him for an immediate report as to what could be done. So far as my hon. friend the Minister of

Railways is concerned, I do not see what pressure he could bring to bear on the railway company which would have any material effect, as at present the local officials of the railway are doing everything they possibly can. When a large bridge is carried away and four or five miles of road are under water, the House can see that the situation is one very difficult to cope with. The transfer is being made across this gap at present by ferries or boats, and our officers are at Regina doing whatever is possible to meet the emergency. Whatever we can do, my hon. friend may rely on being done.

As this railway traverses the greater portion of my constituency, I would like to say a few words before this debate is concluded. Before I make any remarks, I want to allude to the fact that the argument laid before the House by the hon. member for Western Assiniboia cannot be refuted by any one- and I notice that hon. gentlemen opposite have tried to draw a red herring across the trail by raising a point of order about anonymous letters.
I rise to a point of order. There is nothing before the House, and we are wasting its time to no purpose.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I may say that it has been customary, during this and other sessions, for hon. members' to rise and declare their intention of moving the adjournment in order to put themselves in order. Although it would be more regular that the motion to adjourn should be moved and seconded before an hon. gentleman proceeds with his remarks, it has been the custom on both sides for the hon. members to delay making the motion until they concluded what that had to say. I think, therefore, we had better not find fault with that way of proceeding at present.

But the point I make is that the hon. gentleman after declaring that he intended to conclude his remarks with a motion to adjourn, failed to do so. He was either ashamed or forgot to make the motion to adjourn, and consequently there is nothing before the House.
If necessary, I shall move the adjournment of the House.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Better have a seconder.
Seconded by the hon. member for West Assiniboia.
That hon. gentleman cannot second the motion, as he has already spoken.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: I will second the motion.

I want to draw attention to the fact that when the hon. member for
Lanark left the House

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: The hon. gentleman is out of order. He is discussing a question which has just been discussed.
I have a perfect right to reply to the statements made in this debate by the hon. member for Lincoln. I have moved the adjournment of the House, and I think I have the floor.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There was an irregularity came in at an earlier stage. My attention was otherwise occupied when the hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) finished his speech. He was the proper person to move the adjournment, because he said he would. It is a little out of order, probably, for another gentleman to move the adjournment when half the debate had taken place. But I think the House will overlook that and allow the debate to go on.
No, we want the law ; we want your ruling, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If we are to have the law, then I would point out that, as motion was not made before, and so the hon. gentleman (Mr. Haggart) had nothing to discuss.
And he discussed nothing.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the point is raised, I shall be obliged to rule that the discussion previous to the moving of the adjournment is out of order. But that is past and gone and we cannot recall it. We now put ourselves in order by the hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) moving the adjournment, seconded by the hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Calvert).
Are we to understand, Sir, that you allowed this House to go on for an hour and a half with a discussion which was all out of order?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I would answer that in this way :	It was no more
out of order than the procedure we usually adopt. I remarked to a member the other day that our procedure in these cases is not a proper one, because an hon. gentleman might make a long speech intending to conclude with a motion to adjourn, and then find no seconder for his motion. But it is a procedure that has been approved by both sides, and I do not think it would be right for one side to find fault with the other under these conditions.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I rise to a point of order. I came in as you were giving your ruling, Mr. Speaker, and heard what you said. I understand that the hon. member for West Assiniboia read letters reflecting upon the conduct of an hon. member of this House. I understand that the rules of this House prohibit the reading of letters-
That was settled.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: That point was not raised.
If that has been ruled, I would much like to know what your ruling is, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The point was not raised at the time. Another point was raised, as to whether the hon. member was compelled, after reading a private document, to lay it on the table. And, during the discussion of that point of order the other was referred to, but if it was raised as a point of order, I did not notice it. It must have been raised some minutes after the occasion had arisen. Hon. members will understand that, if a point of order is to be raised, it must be raised immediately upon the occurrence of the violation of the rule which is complained of. If there was any irregularity, I did not notice when it took place. It must have taken place some minutes before attention was called to it.

If I might be permitted to resume, I am sure the settlers of the western country, the portion of western Assiniboia and Saskatchewan especially affected, will be pleased to see that when an attempt is made to discuss these matters hon. gentlemen on the other side do every thing in their power to check that discussion, so that the people of the Dominion may not be seized of the facts. The hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) when he attempted to discuss the question, was interrupted constantly, and when I attempt to speak, every point of order that hon. gentlemen can think of is raised. I am sure, as I say, that the people of that country will note with pleasure the efforts of hon. gentlemen opposite to prevent the discussion of this subject which is of such great importance to them. It may not be regarded as of great importance by hon. gentlemen opposite, but there is no more important question for the people of that western country. These hon. gentlemen may not be aware that no less than 200.000 square miles of territory is served by the Regina, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway, to say nothing of the territory served by the Calgary and Edmonton road. As a matter of fact, neither of these roads should ever have been built. Some thirteen years ago, before these roads were built, but after the unfortunate rebellion brought about by the bungling of hon. gentlemen opposite, it was found necessary to build railways into that country. The people in Prince Albert, where I live, the largest town in Saskatchewan, and one of the largest in the Northwest Territories, sent a delegation to the government of that day to secure the extension of the Manitoba and Northwestern Railway into that section. Had that road been assisted to the same extent as these roads were, it would have
been built at once, and would have traversed the beautiful country now being opened up by the Canadian Northern. And it would have been in Edmonton in a few years, and we should not have heard of these other roads. Why was not this done ? Had the Manitoba and Northwestern been extended from Portage la Prairie where it had connection with the Northern Pacific, it would have been built through to the mountains and would have been a great portion of another transcontinental line. That did not suit the Canadian Pacific Railway or those who supported the Canadian Pacific Railway. They did not want to open up another line and bring down the traffic to a connection with the Northern Pacific. They wanted to build feeders for themselves in the shape of branch lines. Had they got the ordinary subsidy of $2,000 a mile in cash, there would have been no very great objection. But they received G.400 acres of land per mile-arable land, fine, fat acres capable of producing wheat; nothing but the choicest would do them- and, on top of that $80,000 a year for carrying in the mails. This being the case, we cannot but come to the conclusion that they received more than was necessary, even at that time, for building the road. But, when so great a subsidy was given, it is only reasonable to say that the government of the day should have seen to it that the road was properly constructed and that it was run in such a way as to give efficient service to the people. But that was not done. The company have sold the land for an average, certainly, of not less than $3 an acre ; they have sold the town sites ; they have received the grant carrying in the mails. And, after all what do we find ? We find to-day a road practically useless-a lot of rotten ties ; old rotten bridges ; old locomotives that should be in the scrap-heap ; no coal ; no water-tanks. I submit that it is not out of place for the representatives of the people of that part of the country to come to this House and ask where all the money from the sale of lands has gone.
