Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at six o'clock I was dealing with the question which had been brought up on the motion to adjourn ; that is, the management and operation of the Calgary and Edmonton and the Regina, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railways. I was endeavouring to show the House that the letters which my hon. friend from West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) read before he took his seat had no direct bearing on the question at issue between my hon. friend and the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier). It was not necessary that these letters should be put in to prove the case which my hon. friend attempted to make and in fact did make against the hon. member for West Toronto. The letters were read merely as a statement in connection with the way the bonds had been sold and the way the land grant had been manipulated. The facts, as far as the Calgary and Edmonton road are concerned, remain unquestionable that the bonds were sold to build that road and that a surplus was left over from the side of the bonds sufficient to
pay the interest for a great many years. The land grant was exempt from liability on account of the bonds by a special clause in the mortgage deed so that the people who purchased these bonds, the bondholders, had no interest in that land whatever. The road has been operated by the Canadian Pacific Railway people, for, I think thirteen or fourteen years, at all events since the road was constructed. It was allowed to run into disrepair ; no betterments had been made upon it at all and the question now arises : Why has that been so ? The Canadian Pacific Railway bought the road a year ago, taking the bonds at one hundred cents on the dollar and the stock at a percentage so that all of this land, amounting to 6,400 acres per mile which was given by the government to aid the construction of the road, remains unaccounted for. Then, there is the $80,000 a year which was given for carrying the mails, and w'hich, I suppose, was used for the purpose of paying interest. The hon. member for West Toronto said that he did not benefit financially by any of these transactions, but still, it must surprise hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House as well as on this side of the House to find that the land company that got the largest portion of the Calgary and Edmonton land grant, some 800,000 acres, had as one of its directors the hon. member for West Toronto. It must also surprise the House to find that a large quantity of this land was given to the firm of Osier, Hammond and Nanton, of which the hon. member for West Toronto is the senior partner. I think in all fairness, considering that these roads have been so liberally subsidized by the government of Canada, that the government have given something like $20,000 a mile to aid in their construction and that the roads are now in a state of disrepair, we ought to be told what has become of all this money. That is what we are trying to find out. What has become of the money that was realized from the sale of these lands ? If that had been used for the purpose of keeping these roads in repair and putting in good modern iron bridges with concrete piers we would not have existing to-day the state of affairs that we are complaining of. This is a serious state of affairs. The Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway traverses a country which comprises about 200,000 square miles. Settlers are scattered all over it; there must be 60,000 people in that neighbourhood. There are the towns of Lumsden, Craik, Hanley, Davidson. Dun-durn, Saskatoon, Osier, Hague, Rosthern, .Duck Lake, Prince Albert and Battleford which are depending for their supply upon this one line of railway, and the settlers in that country are in turn depending on these towns for their supplies. The House heard the telegram which my hon. friend from West Assiniboia read this afternoon. A large number of people went in there and

tools! up homesteads last year. They did a little breaking, got their shanties up, and got their land ready so as to be able to put in some crop this spring. They go back to their homes in the United States, Ontario or Quebec, and sell out their holdings there. Somb of them are poor people. Some have gone to the west to make new homes for themselves. They go up and are stranded at Regina without any money to pay then-expense or to purchase the things which they require. They cannot get in to sow any crop, they cannot get any seed in the ground, and they cannot get a crop for another year. They have sold out their old homes and they have been looking forward to the prospect of being able to make new homes for themselves in the west. This is a very serious state of affairs and one that calls for some remedy at the hands of this House. It may be asked : What is the remedy ? The government know the facts of the case. They know what the roads cost. The road, as: I have pointed out before, is 253 miles long and I want to say right here that the road could have been built over a route 190 miles: in length through a better country, but, the more miles, the more acres of land. The acres were broad, the acres were fat and the more miles of road constructed the more rake-off. Estimating the land at $3 per acre the company received something like $19,000 a mile in land and if they could add 60 miles to the length of the road they got that much more land. I remember on one occasion hearing of an American taking a contract for building a road for the Sultan of Turkey, between two given points. The distance was 90 miles, but the Sultan made the contract at so much per mile and when the bill came in there was a claim for 250 miles of road. The contractor was making a good profit and he ran the road like a snake. I am informed that the railway in Prince Edward Island is so crooked that the conductor can shake hands with the engineer going around some of the curves. This is explained by the fact that that road was built some years ago by the old government and I suppose there were some jobs in it like this road we are discussing. The Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway could have been built, as I have said, over a route 190 miles in length and if that route had been selected there would have been no objection to a subsidy of $3,200 per mile. But, I submit that the road was not needed. It was a piece of jobbery from beginning to end. A gentleman, writing over his own signature in the Toronto ' Globe ' some years ago, addressed an open letter to the hon. member for West Toronto in which he said that it had been conceived in sin. Nobody wanted the road. The people in my part of the country did not want it. They wanted the Manitoba and Northwestern extended up through to Prince Albert so as Mr. DAVIS.
to give them connection with the Northern Pacific and so that the whole of the Saskatchewan valley would be opened up. But, this road was built so that a certain number of gentlemen could get a graft for themselves. The gentlemen connected with the road may ask : What right have the people of Prince Albert to kick ? With all the land that was given by the government to aid in the construction ofi that road and with the mail contract of $80,000 a year any reasonable man would have been satisfied to build the road, because after all, it was only a mud road. There has never been any ballast put on it up to the present time ; it is n mud road and nothing more. One would have expected that when they approached a town they would have continued the railway into the town, but this was not a part of the policy of the gentlemen who built that road. Settlers went in and established towns, trekked over the prairie, brought in their effects, built up the towns and invested their money in them. You would naturally have thought that the gentlemen promoting this railway would have built into these towns. Not a bit of it. When they came to the town of Saskatoon they went across the river, established a town site of their own and sold their lots. They did the same thing in Duck Lake. They compelled the people of Duck Lake to move about two miles up to the road so that they might have a town site at their disposal. When they approached Prince Albert, the biggest town on the Saskatchewan, and one of the largest in the Northwest Territories, they remained outside of the town and told the property owners that if they did not give them half of their lots they would not go to the town at all. As a consequence the people of Prince Albert had to hand over half of their property to these people out of which they have been making money ever since and that on top of all the money they got out of the government. Surely they have reason to kick. Now, the position of things is this :	The
road is in - a worse condition than it was when it was built fourteen years ago. There has been an occasional tie put in, but the majority of the ties are rotten and the culverts are old. The bridge at Saskatoon was fourteen years old when it was carried away a short time ago and every one knows that the ordinary life of a wooden bridge is ten years. The company have no motive power, no coal, no water and the consequence is that they have not carried a pound of freight since January over that road. The people are without supplies and cannot get anything in. When spring comes on this old bridge at Saskatoon goes out. It went out two or three years ago and they cobbled it up again. They might have known that When an ice jam came along it would go out again. These difficulties would have been avoided if they had taken ordinary precautions to see that this bridge was all right.

They did not do so. I suppose because they do not care.
The Calgary and Edmonton has bean taken over by the Canadian Pacific Railway, and I suppose that in their own interests they will operate the road properly. The question remains : who got the land grant ? That question has been discussed by my hon. friend (Mr. Scott) this afternoon, and I venture to say here and now, that it will take the member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) all his time to answer the statements made by my hon. friend (Mr. Scott). If they have got the money out of the land, and the C.P.R. bought it, nothing more is to be said, but these people still have the Qu'Ap-pelle and Long Lake road in their hands and surely there should be some power in the hands of the government to compel them to give some return for the vast sums of money and the vast grants of land we have given to these people for the construction of the road. In order to show how the people in my part of the country feel about it, I wish to read the following resolution which was passed by the town council of Prince Albert:
Resolution of Council of the Town of Prince Albert.
Whereas from the end of the first week in February to the present time there has been great irregularity in the delivery of the mails to this town, periods of twelve days having elapsed between delivery of mails, and at this date this town has received no mail since April 14th, and we are informed that no mail will be received or sent out until some time next week.
And whereas, from February the 10th, until March 10th, the merchants of this town and *district have suffered great loss of business through the inability of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to deliver the freight ordered *and shipped over their railway, and destined for this town.
And whereas large quantities of freight shipped from Winnipeg and eastern points for this town during the months of January, February and March, are still undelivered and the railway company can give our merchants no definite idea as to when these shipments will be delivered, and we are now' informed that the *company has notified its agents to refuse all freight billed for this town.
And whereas at this date the railway bridge *over the South Saskatchewan river at Saskatoon has been swept away-, thus effectually blocking all transportation to this tow'n, and preventing the receipt of any mail, freight or other commodities, and causing to our citizens an almost entire loss of this season's trade.
And whereas there are now five steamboats under construction in this town, and the engines, boilers and other machinery to be used therein have been long since shipped, but are still undelivered and the railway company cannot now-deliver the same for many weeks, thus causing enormous loss to the owners of the said boats and great detriment to their trade.
And whereas the owners of several sawmills in this town have made provisions for the installation of new- machinery in their mills, "which machinery is in the hands of the railway company and is still undelivered, and the non-delivery of which will probably throw a large number of men out of employment.
And whereas there are now at Regina a Jarge number of settlers on their way to this district, who cannot get transportation, owing to the sweeping away of the said bridge at Saskatoon, and who will in all pobability lose this season's crop, owing to the failure of the railway company to provide transportation to bring them from Regina to Prince Albert in time to put in their crop.
And whereas the country through which the survey of the Canadian Northern Railw-ay runs to Prince Albert has never to the knowledge of the oldest inhabitant of this district experienced the severe snow storms which frequent the country between Saskatoon and Regina.
Therefore, be it resolved that this council in council assembled calls the attention of the Dominion government to the severe loss suf-'"T'sd by the citizens of this town and vicinity from the great lack of adequate railway facilities, and urge most strongly upon the government the absolute necessity of securing the construction of the Canadian Northern Railway from Melfort to Prince Albert during the coming summer.	[DOT]
Dated at Prince Albert this 23rd day of April, A.D. 1904.	.
W. J GILMOUR,	C. 0. DAVIDSON, .
Mayor.	Secretary-Treasurer."
This resolution shows the anxiety of the people to have another railway built in the town in the near future, and they refer to the fact that the Canadian Northern should be built from the town of Melfort, eighty miles east of Prince Albert. I wish to read also the following resolution adopted by a meeting of the ratepayers of the town of Prince Albert held in the town hall, April 27th, 1904 :
Moved by Wm. Cowan, Esq., seconded by R. H. Hall, Esq., and adopted unanimously.
Be it resolved,-
1.	That the great importance of constructing a joint railway and traffic over the South Saskatchewan river be brought to the immediate attention of the government, and all possible pressure be used to induce it to carry on this work.
2.	That it is of the utmost importance to the development of Prince Albert, town and district, that the Canadian Northern Railway should be built to this point at the earliest possible moment, and that it is urgently desired that the government should bring all the pressure in its power to bear upon the said railway company to complete their line to this town by the opening of the immigration season of 1905.
3.	That in the event of the government agreeing as in the case of the town of Edmonton, to arrange for the building of a joint railway and traffic bridge over the Saskatchewan river at Prince Albert this meeting place itself on record as in favour of the town giving a cash bonus of $25,000 towards the construction of such a bridge.
The hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) at one time stated in the House that this road never paid. Well, the road never could pay. Mr. Hugh Sutherland of Win-

nipeg, who was connected with the Hudson Bay Railway, and who is well known in railway circles, wrote a letter to say that this railway was conceived in sin. It was built through a section of the country where it should not have been built. They could have reached the town of Prince Albert in a straight line of 190 miles through a good country, but they built 253 miles through a country that was not considered the very best and they never intended that the railway should pay. When they started operating the railway, they charged five cents (5 cents) a mile, and I want mv hon. friend from York (Mr. Maclean) to take notice of that fact. The freight rates were so high that people could haul their produce by team cheaper than they could by the railroad.
For the first forty miles of that road, you could hire teams to haul any commodity for far less money than you could have it hauled on that railway. At the rate of five cents a mile commerciol travellers and business men could not travel, nor could they send freight either. We had four sawmills in our town, but the rate on lumber was so high that they could 'not do business. We have timber there and could have supplied the prairie country with fuel, but the railway company made the rates so high that they apparently did not want to do business. The British Columbia members may talk about their lumber mills not being able to do business, but they never had any such experience as our lumbermen had ; they had to wait until the country in the vicinity of the mills was settled before they could sell any lumber at all. Now, Mr. Speaker, the railway commission may have power to settle this matter, but at all events, we should get relief in some way. Why should we pay them $80,000 for carrying the mails, if the mails are not carried ? There should be a commission appointed to inevstigate who got the land. They received enough from the proceeds of the sale of the bonds to build the road and leave a nice little surplus in addition to that. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Osier) said that they had to sell enough bonds to borrow money to pay back the interest. That may be financing, but if it is I do not know anything about it. If I went to the bank to borrow $500, and if they knew I had to borrow the money to pay the interest, I think they would look at me twice before sending me the money. Anyway, there was enough money left here to pay the interest for six yars on the bonds, and half a million dollars besides. We cannot get any track of that. It went for miscellaneous expenditure I suppose, or perhaps some of it went into the fund we hear about in Ontario, where each candidate got $500.
But I would like to know where all the money went; it certainly did not go into the Mr. DAVIS.
road. Now, I hope the government or the railway commission will deal with this matter. I know that the bargain was made fast and close with these railway companies. Talk about the bargain that we are now making with the Grand Trunk Pacific people; it is nothing to this bargain that was made for the benefit of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. A statesman would have built the railway up through the heart of the Saskatchewan valley to Edmonton, where there was a good country that would have rapidly been settled ; but it was located away to the south, and these two branches were built, and the Canadian Pacific Railway got the benefit. Something should be done to give the people relief, and done at once, Even though they are able to cross the river by a ferry, and get no crops, w bat can they keep themselves and their families on till next year ? Although tne bridge has been down for a month or more,
I Relieve nothing has yet been done to-v ards building a new one. I think something should be done to compel these people to put that road into proper repair at once. With reference to the controversy between my hon. friend from West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) and the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier), it does not interest me to any great extent, it is the operation of the road that interests me. When any of those who represent western constituencies have the courage to get up in this House and attack the Canadian Pacific Railway and demand redress for the grievances of the people, we know that we are taking our political lives in our hands. We know that the hon. member for West Toronto and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company cannot turn many votes against us as they employ few men there; but they have other means. This gentleman who was secretary-treasurer of a fund that supplied $500 to each candidate in Ontario may be able to raise a fund to supply $10,000 or $15,000 to each candidate in the Northwest. We know that we have all these things to contend against; but so long as I have a seat in this House, I am prepared to defend the interests of the settlers at large. I am not here for the purpose o? hiding the fault of corporations, no matter what corporations they may be. I have seen the hon. member for West Toronto hold up his hands in holy horror a the idea of granting any more railway subsidies; he thought it was time they were done away with. But last year a subway was brought I down to this House for 136 miles of a

Canadian Pacific Railroad, and I noticed Hat the hon. member for West Toronto *was not here to protest against it. He was conspicuous by bis absence. The bon. member for West Assiniboia moved to strike out tbe subsidy, and I am sorry tbe hon. member for West Toronto is not here to second the resolution. I am not kicking against that subsidy. It was right to grant it. I have no objection to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company getting a subsidy if they give some return for the money. 1 have never opposed that company getting a subsidy ; but when a member of this House who says it is wrong to give subsidies and who is one of the leading directors of a company w^hich applies for a subsidy, is not in his place to oppose that subsidy, it looks to me as if it depend 2d very much on whose ox wTas gored. If the grist was running into the Canadian Pacific Railway mill, it was all right; but if it was running into any other mill, it was all wrong
Was there any penalty clause put into that subsidy to prevent a recurrence of conditions similar to those which the hon. gentleman is now describing ?

Since this government has held office, all these things have been looked after. If my hon. friend will look at the railway legislation that has been passed in this House since 1896, and compare 't with what went before, the scales will cliop from his eyes.
Is there a penalty clause ?

The principle of government control was adopted by this government for the first time, and, as my hon. friend knows, every precaution has been taken to safeguard the interests of the settlers. Let him consider the legislation that was passed last session with reference to prairie fires, drainage across railways, cattle-guards, the carriage of mails, and other matters, and compare it with the railway legislation of hon. gentlemen opposite when they were in power, and he will see that this government has taken every precaution to safeguard the interests of the settlers. If my hon. friend will show me anything in this Act regarding the Qu'-Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway, intended to provide any protection for the rights of the people, I would like him to show it to me.
I do not say there is.

Let him look at the Act re garding the Calgary and Edmonton Railway; will he find anything there to protect the interests of the people in any way ? He will not find any charter passed during the time hon. gentlemen opposite were in power S9

in which the interests of the people were safeguarded in any way. And yet when legislation is introduced giving the government full control over railroads in the interests of the people, these hon. gentlemen are ready to carp at it. I am sorry that I have had to take up so much of the time of tbe House ; but this is a very serious mat-tei for the people whom I have the honour to represent, when you take into consideration the fact that since the month of January they have not had any freight. The town of Prince Albert has 3,500 people ; the towns of Duck Lake, Rosthern, Saskatoon, are all large and flourishing towns ; and they all ha-ve to suffer because the people who own these railways allowed them to get into that state. We need more railways in the Northwest, and the sooner we get them the better ; and when we facilitate the Grand Trunk Pacific or any other independent line being constructed, for the purpose of affording competition with the roads which we have been discussing to-day, such a policy is popular with every one in the western country. I hope the government will do what they can to get the Canadian Northern constructed into Prince Albert this year, and also as far west as possible towards Battleford and Edmonton ; because I believe the people will never get the relief they require until that road is built. We do not suppose now that a bridge will be built. We can'not expect the poor bondholders, the widows and orphans who have invested their money in this railway, to build a bridge. They put their money in, thinking they were going to get some return for it, but I do not think they got anything, the grafters got it. Where is the money to come from to build the bridge unless we can make the people who sold these lands disgorge ? If that can be done, I hope it will be done at once. Again, let me say :	If the government can do
anything to have the Canadian Northern built to Prince Albert and also built w estward to Battleford and Bdmonton this season,-1 hope that it will be done. We have 60,000 people in that part of the country, and the question is whether we want to keep them there or not. They have all taken up homes. Many of them are not wealthy people, and something should be done to afford them relief without delay.
If the Canadian Northern people could be induced to build through that country at once, and give the people relief, their action would be looked upon as a god-send to the settler in the district of Saskatchewan and Northern Assiniboia.

Has the Minister of Agriculture, or the government, any information regarding the claim of one Hubert F. Page, of Matsqui, B.C., against the United States government for a refund of the duty improperly charged him on a consignment of horses for breeding purposes, sent into that country ? If so, has the claim been paid ? If not paid, is the government pressing the claim, and in what shape does the matter now stand ?
Hon. SYDNEY' FISHER (Minister of Agriculture) :
In April 1902 the Minister of Agriculture was informed by Mr. H. F. Page, of Mission, B.C., that on certain pure bred Percheron horses which he had imported from British Columbia into the state of Washington duties had been exacted by the United

States customs authorities, contrary to the provisions of the United States tariff, and the good offices of this government were asked to obtain a refund of this duty from the United States government. Mr. Page was thereupon requested to make his representations fully, which having been done, the same were communicated by the Secretary of State through the British Embassy at Washington to the United States authorities. Mr. Page had previously appealed from the decision of the local United States custom authorities in the state of Washington to the Board of the United States General Appraisers.
In December, 1902, the Treasury Department through the Department of State of the United States replied to the British Ambassador giving the decision of the Board of United States General Appraisers on Mr. Page's appeal, from which the following is an extract:
' Under paragraph 473 of the Tariff Act of July 24, 1897, these animals, it is claimed, should have been admitted free of duty as animals " imported specially for breeding purposes." The appraisers hold, however, that in view of Mr. Page's own statements of the advertisement of his horses for sale before he imported them, and of his immediate sale of some of them, they could not be held to have been imported " specially for breeding purposes." They must be held to have been imported for the purpose of sale. The fact that they were pure bred horses could not affect the purpose for which they were imported or the intent of the importer. It is held to be immaterial whether Mr. Page intended that the purchasers of his horses should use them for breeding purposes or other purposes. He did not intend them for that purpose. He intended them for sale.'
The action of the collector in the state of Washington was consequently sustained. The reply further stated that the matter had passed out of the province of the 'Treasury Department, but that Mr. Page had an appeal to the courts. This reply was communicated to Mr. Page.
This government has taken no further action in the matter and is not aware whether the claim has been paid or not.
In April, 1903. the paragraph 473 of the tariff above referred to was amended to read as follows :
' Any animal imported by a citizen of the United States specially for breeding purposes shall be admitted free whether intended to be so used by the importer himself or for sale for such purpose, &c., &c.'
At the time of the importation this article read as follows :
' Any animal imported specially for breeding purposes shall be admitted free.'

For a return showing all papers, letters, petitions and resolutions in reference to payments of claims for losses arising out of the Rebellion of 1885, in the Northwest Territories.

He said : I have had the pleasure, Mr. Speaker, of bringing a resolution on practi cally the same lines before to the attention of this House on a previous occasion. Last year before the Close of the session I brought this question before the House, and I remember that I was then severely taken to task by the members of the opposition for bringing it up, as they said, in the last days of the session. I was also taken to task by lion, members opposite, including the hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden), because I had not given sufficient notice. They said that I brought the question up, made certain statements about certain parties, and that they had not time to look into the papers and find out if these statements were correct. I intend to make the very same statements that I made at that time, but this year I placed this motion on the order paper at the opening of the session, so that hon. gentlemen opposite have had about a month and a half in which to look into this question and to be seized of all the facts in relation to it. Thus, if there is anything in my speech which they think is incorrect, they will be in a position to put me straight. This question, it is true, is a little ancient, but the rights of the people should never be neglected, even if close upon twenty years have elapsed since the unfortunate rebellion in the Northwest took place.
There are certain people in that part of the country who have claims against the government for compensation for lossess incurred at that time. They do not consider that they were fairly treated and they insist on having these claims brought before this House. I, as the representative of these people, have no apology to offer the House for bringing the question before the House again, because in doing so I am simply endeavouring to promote the interests of the people of the constituency I represent. We have to establish, in the first place, the question as to who is responsible for the rebellion. The people up there who have lost certain property by the rebellion are putting in claims for compensation for their losses and therefore we must establish that the government were to blame for bringing about that rebellion. I think we can establish that successfully. There are certain petitions that we would like to have got hold of that were sent to the government by the people of Saskatchewan, letters that were sent by government officials in the Saskatchewan country and letters that were sent by leading citizens of Saskatchewan previous to the rebellion breaking out. I would like to have been able to have produced those letters and petitions and given them to the House, but, unfortunately, we have not been able to get our hands on them. There is a rumour in circulation which is generally believed that at a certain time previous to this government taking power, a bonfire was kindled in the office of the Minister of the Interior. We
have heard of the ancients offering up sacrifices so that the smoke might bear their prayers up to the heavens, but in this case we have some privy councillors in the office of the Minister of the Interior offering up a sacrifice of certain petitions, letters and communications from the people of the Northwest Territories, which, if preserved, would have plainly shown that the government were responsible for the unfortunate rebellion.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not the present Minister of the Interior.

Not the present Minister of the Interior. I mentioned the fact that it was before this government came into power. I suppose they found that it was not convenient to carry off these documents. The petitions and letters which had been sent to the government were so numerous and so bulky that they could not very well carry them away in their grip sacks or their pockets, so that it was necessary to make a bonfire and this bonfire took place surrounded by certain members of His Majesty's Privy Council. Therefore, we are not in possession of these petitions, but I lived in that country previous to the rebellion and know the circumstances under which these petitions were sent. I know that they were sent down. I have seen the letters that were sent down and I know whereof I speak. I know that in 1882 a very large petition was sent down from that part of the country signed by all the half-breeds of the South Saskatchewan river setting forth the grievances of which they complained at that time. In the early days in Manitoba the half-breeds had settled on river lots ten chains wide. They had built their houses along the river front and were living there. When they moved into the Northwest Territories to the Saskatchewan river, the half-breeds adopted the same system and built their houses along the river front. When the government took over the country they sent up their surveyors and in place of surveying the land into ten chain lots, they insisted on surveying it into quarter sections, so that two, three and four families were collected together on one quarter section. The people objected to that. They said that the country belonged to them, that it had been the domain of their forefathers, and that the government had taken possession of it. The rights of the half-breeds had been recognized in Manitoba, and they asked why they should not be treated the same as the half-breds in Manitoba had. The answer they got to that petition was that when the proper time came each case would be dealt with on its merits, but, the proper time never came and the cases were never dealt with on their merits. Another question was the question of scrip. We know that they had a rebellion in Manitoba for which the government of that day were responsible. The government sent up a governor before they

liad consulted the people of Manitoba, and the people wanted to know how they were going to be treated and the result was that a rebellion was brought about. One of the principal causes of the rebellion in the Northwest was the question of scrip. The people there said that the children of the halfbreeds in Manitoba had been given scrip. The half-breeds of the Northwest Territories who had nothing to do with the half-breeds of Manitoba had not been treated with at all. The government in place of treating with them took possession of their country, started with their surveyors to survey the land, to cut these people's holdings up and throw them in all together without consulting the people and without giving them scrip. Petition after petition was sent down to the government of the day and indignation meetings were held with the result that the halfbreeds sent over for Riel. All this was known to the government. It was going on for six months and the government took no action in the matter at all. As a consequence the rebellion broke out. All the loyal citizens were rounded up in the town. All the farmers and settlers around Prince Albert were rounded up, brought in by the authorities and not allowed to look after their property. Their property was destroyed but they expected that they would receive compensation for it. To show that the government were to blame for the rebellion, I want to recite this fact. The half-breeds asked that their lands should be surveyed in river lots and that scrip should be given to their children. These two requests were refused by the government and the rebellion was brought about, resulting in an immense loss in blood and treasure. The rebellion was hardly settled when the government sent out to treat with these people and gave them what they had asked for before the rebellion had broken out. If they had done this six months before there would have been no rebellion at all. These people were only asking what was right because the government gave into their demands, gave them scrip and surveyed their lands. During the time this rebellion was in progress the people were brought into town and not allowed to look after their property. They had their houses burned and their horses carried away. The conduct in connection with the suppression of the rebellion was anything but creditable to the people of this country. The property of the people was loaded into boats and carried off. I do not blame the soldiers, but, the hangers on, loaded the peoples' billiard tables on steamboats and took them to Winnipeg. Whole bands of horses were driven off and some of these horses are around Stony Mountain yet. The cattle were collected and driven off ; in fact they drove off or carried away everything in sight. These people ask for compensation for that loss.
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend (Mr. Pope) says ' hear, heai\ ' I hope he is going to support me in trying to get the claims of these settlers adjusted. When the rebellion was over the government recognized their liability by appointing a commission ostensibly to adjust these claims, to And out who had lost property and who had not lost property, and to see that those who had lost anything received payment. We supposed that that is what the government appointed the commission for. But later on we discovered that they had other objects in view, They appointed on that commission a resident settler, a native of the country. He was put on the commission as a local man who would see that people got justice and that there would be no room for complaint. The first commission that sat paid off a certain number of claims. I notice in the report of the claims settled by the first commission of which this resident gentleman was a member, that a majority of his relatives were liberally dealt with while other people came off without getting what they considered proper compensation.
After the first award the people asked to have the question opened again, and the commision was reappointed, and took evidence in several hundred claims. But they did not make an award, and why ? In the meantime an Act had been passed giving representation to the Northwest Territories, and the district of Saskatchewan where the rebellion took place was to have a representative, and in November we were informed that an election would take place, during the winter the commission adjourned and the local commissioner came back to Prince Albert early in the winter, and started to organize the campaign for the Conservative party. We asked if he were a claims commissioner still ; if he was sitting in judgment on us, and if we were to look to him to get justice, but we did not get any information. They were bound by hook or crook to carry the constituency to show that they were not to blame for the rebellion. I do not know where the money came from, but the people up there know that there was no less than $40,000 dumped into that constituency. This commissioner canvassed from house to house, and addressed public meetings.
Who was he ?
His name was Mr. McKay if you want to know.
Yes, I know him.

He canvassed from door to door, the people were told that if they wanted to get their claims paid they should vote Conservative. Then there was a little Tory lawyer who was in the town of Prince Albert; his name was W. V. McLeace, and he announced through a circular that if people wanted to get their claims paid they would have to vote for the Tories.
Hear, hear.
My bon. friend says ' hear, hear.' He doesn't like to hear some of these facts, but he will hear some more of them.
Come on again.
