You see he got $5 a day returning to Prince Albert when he was coming to do election work ; he was travelling in style. Then he has in his account a lot of ' &c.'s ' and ' &c.'s ' ; a job lot for $1,338.96, making a total of $14,498.96 ; I tell you. The election was held in March, 1887.
No ; February, 1887.

You can have it in February if you like. This gentleman was paid straight through the year and this thing occurred in the middle of the year, so it does not make any difference. This gentleman was electioneering and canvassing, and he was paid $20 a day of the people's money. Just imagine this gentleman getting on the public platform and addressing the poor electors and his hands on the $20 paid by the government. The people who listened to him did not know that he was pocketing the $20 a day. This was the gentleman who was claims commissioner. Was it honest to take $20 a day, Sundays included, and put it in his pocket when he was acting as a heeler and stumper for the Conservative party ?
No.
My hon. friend says it was not honest.
I even doubt if it is true.

Well, I will show you whether it is true or not. There are hundreds of the people in my country know it is true, and when the great majority of the people say it is true there must be something in it. I was at the meetings addressed by this gentleman, but in the innocence of my heart I did not know at that time that he was getting $20 a day, and if I did I would have made it hot for him.
Perhaps he will give you a chance yet.
No. Not much.
Don't brag.

I am not in the habit of bragging. You will have to send a little more of the Canadian Pacific Railway money with him than he has got now, although it is reported that be is handling it, before he can beat me, I can tell you that. He will need to pay another visit to the member for Toronto's private car in Winnipeg before he will be able to defeat me. This gentleman was acting as a political stumper, organizer and canvasser. At that time it was open voting. He and his people who were in charge of the elections stood at the polls to see how the people voted. After the election was over the gentlemen who voted for the Conservative candidate, no matter what their record had been, were paid large sums of money, and I am here to say right now, that they were paid for claims that were only myth, while people who had lost a lot of property and who voted as their conscience told them to vote, had the knife put into them and they did not get paid at all. These people now come before parliament and say that they have not been fairly treated. My hon. friend says he does not believe it, but I will read the petition signed by hundreds of people, and here it is :

The petition of the undersigned settlers of the district of Saskatchewan, in the Northwest Territories, humbly showeth :
That during the Rebellion of 1885 in the Northwest Territories, the said settlers did lose large amount of property for which they have not been compensated. That the government is responsible for said loss, on account of the fact that they ordered all the settlers into the towns of Prince Albert and Battleford and that they were not, therefore, in a position to protect the said property and the same was destroyed.
That the government is responsible,-
1st. That on account of maladministration of western affairs by the government of the day and neglect to answer the petitions of the people rebellion was brought about.
2nd. On account of their taking the settlers away from their homes and not leaving them
2S15

to protect their property, the same was destroyed.
That the government did recognize certain responsibilities by appointing a commission to investigate said claims, that on the said commission a resident of the district was appointed to see that the settlers got justice, that the said commission sat upon the 25th of August, 1885, and on the 6th of January, 1886, that on 'the 18th of December, 1885, the said commission reported in favour of the payment of several claims to the extent of $131,363.35.
That the said commission was further employed to investigate said claims from the 15th of March, 1886, to August 9th, 1887.
That during the time the said commission was appointed and supposed to be sitting, the election of 1887 took place.
That the said claims were investigated, but not paid.
That during the said election campaign, one of the said commissioners, Mr. Thomas McKay, did come into the district of Saskatchewan and act as an organizer for the government of the day. That he spoke at public meetings, canvassed and did everything that was possible for a man to do in the interest of the government candidate for about two months. That the vote was an open vote and that the said McKay was in a position to know how every elector voted.
That during the said election when the said McKay was acting as an organizer and general worker, the said McKay was receiving from the Dominion government a salary to the extent of $15 a day, Sundays included, and $5 a day for living expenses, and his railway fare was paid from Ottawa to Saskatchewan and return by the said government. That after the said election was over, the said partisan, McKay, appeared on the said commission as judge of the claims of the said settlers.
Your petition is, therefore, a claim that the said McKay after taking part in the said election, as above set forth, under pay from the Dominion government, could not render justice to those who voted against the government and did not do so.
That parties who voted for the government got paid in many cases more than they were entitled to and that others who voted against the government got their claims reduced and in the majority of cases got nothing at all.
That all the settlers who put in claims swore to the correctness ol same and the wholesale disallowance of said claims was tantamount to labelling a respectable class of people as perjurers.
Your petitioners, therefore, believe that they did not obtain justice for the reasons above stated, and pray that the government will appoint a commission to look into the facts and render justice to those to whom justice is due.
What is the date of that ?

These petitions were sent to me last week. I got some of them to-day. Here is one from Duck Lake, signed by over forty people. Here is one from Fort a la C-orne, signed by every man" of the district. Grits and Tories are all on that petition.
How many were there at the time of the rebellion ?
They were all there. There are hundreds of names here.
All signed by one hand ?

No, signed by every man io the district-by clergymen and others who knew what they were signing. The names of some of the most respectable people in the district of Saskatchewan are on these petitions.
They are the Conservatives.

My hon. friend may have his own idea about that. I will just read some of the names on one of these petitions. Here is one from Bresaylor, near Battleford, signed by James Bremner, Rev. Philip McDonald, E. J. Spence, David Taylor, W. H. English (Church of England missionary), Rev. H. Delmas, Rev. J. Poulenard (parish priest), and many others. Most of these gentlemen were all there at the time of the rebellion, and were seized of the facts. When my hon. friend from Halton says he is not sure whether the facts I am stating are correct or not, I can tell him that I have the figures here to prove everything I have said. Here is a statement which goes to show that this gentleman who was acting as commissioner was paid for his services and his expenses, including railway fare, during the time that election took place; and I make the statement that he worked for two months, speaking at meetings and doing everything he could to forward the interests of the Conservative candidate, and that during that time he pocketed $20 a day of government money. Knowing how the people would vote, he did not and could not do justice to them. Any one who resides in that part of the country and looks at the list of claims will know that. I have here a list of the claims, and I will comment on a few of the items. I have already mentioned that in the first $131,000 that was paid some of the relatives of the local commissioner were dealt with very generously. A widow woman who lived in Prince Albert was paid on her first claim $2,500 and on her second $2,000. No one around there ever knew where the $4,500 worth of property existed. Many other claims were paid in the same way. A gentleman at Batoche, a Mr. Le-tander-commonly known as ' Batoche,' the place being named after him-had a good deal of influence, and when the election came on he turned it into the Conservative party. What was the result ? $19,000 odd was paid to him for his loss. Another man, a neighbour of his, Mr. Emmanuel Champagne, who lost double what Batoche did, put in an honest claim for $13,310, and he did not get a cent. He said : ' I will not vote for the Tory party if you pay my claim ten times over ; I am not going to sell my principles '; and he never got a cent. Right across the river from Batoche two gentlemen were doing business in a little log store, not more than sixteen feet square, and they lived in the upper part of the building. There was

no railway at that time, and they brought in their stock by ox-team. They had only a few things hanging along the walls, but they were excellent workers in the campaign, and how much do you suppose they got? Something like $13,000 for what was in that littlei building. Everybody in that country knows that the whole stock could have been put on a bob-sleigh, and one horse would have been enough to haul it. If you go through this list you can always see by the ciphers where a man is a Grit.
Hear, hear-every time.

I suppose the bon. gentleman believes that a man who belongs to the opposition party should not get anything. Here is another case of the same kind-Jean Baptiste Boyer, who turned out to be a good Conservative; but be was at the start as great a Reformer as there was in the country. I think he was a member of the half-breed council. He repented of his sins however ; joined the faithful, and put in a claim for $9,344.34, and was allowed $6,461.63. It was worth while, with an open vote, to cast it for the Conservative candidate in that election.
Just previous to that there was another man named Jean Baptiste Arcand, who was a great Grit, and he would not vote for the Conservative candidate. He said to the Conservative : it was you who brought on this rebellion and forced our children to wander through the woods. We lost some of them, who died from exposure and I will never poll a vote for you. Did he get anything ? No, he put in his claim, and let us see what resulted. He put in a claim for $599.15, but he got nothing at all because he did not vote right. Here is another gentleman, Anderson, who refused to vote as the faithful wanted. He put in a claim for $1,000 but three ciphers were put behind his name. There was a gentleman by the name of W. P. BeauprO, who was a well known election heeler at Duck Lake. He was employed in a store and they supposed he had a certain amount of influence. He put in a claim for $7,587.50, and being an excellent man at elections and a good worker, he got $4,606. The next gentleman is James Ballendine. They treated him with a great deal of generosity. They could not convert him, but thought they might soften him. He claimed $126.75 and they gave him the magnificent sum of $8.00. The next gentleman is Gilbert Breland. He put in a claim for $186.75, but as he was unfortunately a Grit, there are three ciphers behind his name. Joseph Corrigall comes next-one of the most honest upright and respectable men in the country, a man not capable of putting his signature to anything that is not true. Well, he put in a claim for $634.60, but because he did not vote right, there are three ciphers opposite his name and he got nothing.
I find here another gentleman by the name of Cromartie, who put in a claim for $2 215. They had some designs on him. They expected they might be able to get him to come back into the fold, and they gave him the magnificent sum of $40, I understand he refused to take it. He said they had better keep it, that he had sworn to the truth, that he had lost every dollar in goods put into the claim, and he was not going to be considered a perjurer and then take $40. I find a gentleman named Joseph Charette, who could not see his way clear to vote straight. The canvassers could not convince him to vote Conservative, so they turned him down and he got nothing. There is another gentleman named Archibald Campbell.
Hear, hear.
There was no chance for him, because he was a good Grit like the hon. member for York. He put in a claim for $311.75.
For cabbage ?

I do not know whether for cabbage, or woodpeckers, or Christmas trees, but he did not get paid, although there was certainly a lot of goods cabbaged from him. Then there is Ambroise Dubois, who claimed $300 and got nothing. Madame Veronique Dumas claimed $556 and got nothing. William Diehl-here is a gentleman who took an active part in suppressing the rebellion. He put in a claim for $135, swore to the truth of his claim, is a decent respectable man, and he got nothing at all. Here is a gentleman by the name of Fidler, sr., of St. Antoines. He put in a claim for $1,695. He is a very respectable man, who lives close to Prince Albert and is well known, and he got nothing because he would not vote right. Edward Fidler and George Fidler put in claims. George put in a claim for $295. He is a decent respectable fellow, who lives there yet, and his name is on one of these petitions as well as his father's. He was told he could not get anything because he did not vote right. Here is a family of Foulds, respectable people, who have lived there many years, One of them put in a claim for $1,000 and got nothing. Alexander Foulds put in a claim for another thousand and got nothing. He would not be believed on his oath. Here is another gentleman, James E. Fidler, who put in a claim for $413. They must have imagined they could do something with James, for they gave him $68. I think they thought they could soften him. Here is another gentleman, Roger Goulet. Everybody knows that all the Goulets were good Tories, he was a relative of the old scrip commissioner in the earlier days and put in a claim for $1,957. He got $1,261. And I venture to say there was not a bigger agitator in Saskatchewan. But he

This letter is dated April 8th of this year, which goes to show that Judge Sedgewick had honestly reported in favour of the payment of a certain amount on that claim and that the government, because they were afraid of opening up some other claims, refused to do justice to this man. I think that after the Deputy Minister of Justice had investigated this claim and had reported in favour of paying a certain amount, the government of the day should have acted on that report and should have paid that amount of money even if it had thereby

opened up these other claims because I do Dot see any reason why other claims should not be opened up. It is never too late to adjust a grievance, and if these people have a just claim it should be looked into and be paid ; if it is not just it will not be paid. They are only asking to have their cases looked into, and if the statements made are true redress their grievances. If you find they are not in accordance with the facts do not pay them. That is a reasonable proposition and that is all that these people ask. Mr. McLean has letters from Sir Donald A. Smith, the present Lord Strathcona, in which he approves of the government paying Mr. McLean a certain amount on this claim. Lord Strathcona was seized of the facts as he was at the head of the Hudson's Bay Company when this unfortunate rebellion took place. Here is a second letter from Sir Donald Smith. Here is a letter from Mr. Scarth, who was afterwards a member of this House, in which he supported the claim of Mr. McLean. I have here a letter from the present Attorney General of Manitoba, Mr. Colin H. Campbell, in which he promises to support the claims and says he will do everything he possibly can to have the claim adjusted. Evidently the promises of these gentlemen did not amount to much. I have a promise of Mr. Campbell, who says he will do all that he can ; Senator Schultz is another. Then there are letters from Mr. Adam Brown, M.P., Mr. Scarth and Mr. R. W. Ross, M.P., promising support. This poor man went junketing on from year to year expecting to have payment, but up to the present time he is just where he was when he started, although he has all this influence behind him. I think these claims should be opened up. If these people have a grievance it is the duty of the government to look into that grievance and if possible to redress it. I suppose there are hundreds of names of respectable people signed to these petitions, in which the statement is made that they were not treated fairly, and that it is desirable to have a commission appointed (to investigate the claims and see that justice is done. I hope the government will take this into their serious consideration, will look into it because there is not the least doubt that there is a strong feeling all through this country resulting from the way these people were treated. The commission was used as a political machine pure and simple.. The man on whom the people depended, the local commissioner, was travelling around stumping at meetings, and taking $20 a day. People said that the reason the government did not pay the claims was because they found it cheaper to buy up the commissioner than pay the people. Now, that there is a change of government they expect that their grievances will be looked into and that justice will be done. Mr. McLean Mr. DAVIS.
was promised by all the Conservative politicians at that time that his claim would be paid. Judge Sedgewick went up and examined the claim of Mr. McLean, and although he reported in favour of a payment, the government, because they thought they might have to pay a few of these other claims, refused to open -up the question at all, and therefore they decided to put a plug in the wheel and to stop the whole proceedings. I hope the government will take the question up, look into it and see that justice is done to to whom justice is due

Nothing but a sense of duty would induce me to rise in the House again to-day, but as a representative of the Northwest, as one having some acquaintance with the facts which have been related by the hon. gentleman from Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) I deem it to be my duty to corroborate, so far as I am able, his statement, and to lend my support to the plea which he has put forward for a very considerable number of the residents of the district of Saskatchewan, wdiich my hon. friend (Mr. Davis) so well represents in this House. Regardless of what may be the view of any person as to the conduct of the chief actors in the deplorable occurrences of 1885 in the Northwest, I think that there can be no difference of opinion that had it not been for the flagrant neglect of the government of the day that most deplorable affair never would have occurred. As my bon. friend (Mr. Davis) has stated, that fact is partly proved by what took place immediately after the suppression of the rebellion. A commission was appointed when it was too late to escape the trouble which had been brought about by neglect and to some extent the grievances of the natives of that country were redressed. But ever since the report of that commission, there has been a feeling in the minds of many people in the Northwest Territories that these rebellion losses claims were not dealt with in the manner in which they should have been dealt with and that the claimants did not receive then-dues as a result of the investigation on the part of the commission which dealt with the matter. I think my hon. friend from Saskatchewan has a very good case to put forward and that he is very well justified in putting forward the plea in behalf of these claimants which he has been arguing this evening. I have a claim in regard to another citizen of the Northwest Territories that I want to present to the government and the House very briefly and on account of the late hour which has now been reached I will not extend my remarks as much as I might otherwise feel disposed to do. I wish to make a plea on behalf of a citizen of this country who at one crisis in the history of Canada rendered very material

service to the Dominion. I refer to a gentleman whose name may be known to most of the members of this House, Mr. Jean Louis LegarS, whose post office address is Willow Bunch and who twenty-five years ago was a trader with the natives of the Northwest Territories at the Wood Mountain police post. Mr. LegarS removed from the province of Quebec about 1860 to the western prairies. At the time the deplorable Ouster massacre occurred across the American border. Mr. Legare had been some sixteen or seventeen years in business as a trader at Wood Mountain. As every one knows, following the Ouster massacre, the Indian Chief, Sitting Bull, with a band of 500 Indians invaded Canada and came to the locality of Wood Mountain. Had it not been for the service rendered at that time by Mr. Legare no one can tell what trouble might have been caused in the country or to the government of Canada. No one can tell what expenditure might have been necessary by the trouble which might have been raised by Sitting Bull and his band of 500 warlike Indians. Fortunately Mr. I.egarG was on the ground and in him was found a man who had already to a very large degree won the confidence of the natives of the country. Up to that time the boundary line did not have the significance that it has at the present time. Mr. Legare's acquaintance extended to the natives south of the 49th parallel as well as to those north of the line. I may say to the House, and there is a considerable number of the hon. gentlemen here who have some acquaintance with Mr. Legare, that between the Atlantic and the Pacific there will not be found a more honest or simple minded man than Mr. LegarS, of Willow Bunch. The natives understood that and had great confidence in Mr. LegarS. Sitting Bull had great confidence in Mr. Legare and as a result of the negotiations that Mr. Legare entered into with Sitting Bull at that time, Sitting Bull consented to go back to the United States and surrender himself to the United States authorities.
About what time was that ?

The year in which Sitting Bull went back and surrendered to the United States was about 1881. It was a considerable time before that year that the Custer massacre occurred and Sitting Bull with his band crossed to the Wood Mountain country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In 1876.
Mr. iSCOTT. It was in 1876, I believe. During the time that Sitting Bull and his Indians were in the Wood Mountain country they lived upon Mr. Legare. Mr. LegarS was a trader and a trader in that district was obliged to have his supplies freighted by Red River cart from Fort Garry, and goods freighted a matter of 500 miles had a
very considerable value in the trader's store. Sitting Bull and his Indians literally ata Mr. Legare out of house and home. They not only consumed the whole year's store and trading supplies but they made it impossible for Mr. Legare in that year to do any business. He fed them out of his store and had no goods left to do business with. He lost a great deal of time as well as the supplies and the entire profits of the year's trading. I may be permitted to read to the House a brief description of what occurred at this time in the Wood Mountain district which I find here upon an official record.
Perhaps the hon. gentleman will tell us what year he is speaking of ? About what year did these occurrences take place ?
In the year 1876.

I submit, Mr. Speaker, that we have wasted enough time to-day and that the hon. gentleman should be kept within the record. The motion has reference to the rebellion losses of 1885 and the question the hon. gentleman is discuss-sing has no reference whatever to the matter before the House. I think you ought to restrain the hon. gentleman and bring him within the record so that there may be some possibility of getting on with the business of the House. I ask for your ruling, Mr Speaker, as to whether he is in order or not in discussing the question he is now speaking about.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The resolution which is now before the House makes special reference to one particular question. I will read it.
Address for a return showing all papers, letters, petitions and resolutions in reference to payments of claims for losses arising out of the Rebellion of 1885 in the Northwest Territories.
I do not really think the discussion of this item is within the four corners of the resolution.

I am obliged to bow to your 1'uling, Mr. Speaker. I am very sorry that the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) has deprived me of this opportunity of bringing forward a good and just claim on behalf of a citizen or this country who is very well entitled to some consideration. I shall have to seek another opportunity of bringing forward this matter on behalf of Mr. LegarS.

I have listened with a good deal of interest to the farce that has been engaged in this evening by the hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) and the hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott). I must confess I am surprised, considering that one of these hon. gentlemen has been sitting in this House since 1896, and the other gentleman since 1900, that they have allowed this important matter to

lie dormant and not called the attention of the government to it, knowing all the facts as they do, I think surely they have very small ground indeed to again appeal to their constituents.
I think the best Conservative literature that could be circulated in their constituencies, is a report of the speeches which these two gentlemen have delivered. If any of my constituents had what I considered just claims, and for seven long years I had sat supporting the government without demanding redress for their grievances and without bringing them to the attention of the government, I assure you I would not expect my constituents to return me. I am not familiar with the facts, and do not know whether these claims are well founded or not, but if they are, then these two hon. gentlemen deserve the censure of this House for not having brought them to the attention of parliament at an earlier date.

speakeroldname: Hon. CLIFFORD SIFTON (Minister of the Interior).
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have no desire to enter into a discussion of the question, but I must say, speaking from recollection, that this matter has been already brought to the attention of parliament. There was the well known case of Bremner furs and other matters discussed in this House some years ago. I am unable to understand on what principle the hon. gentleman (Mr. Henderson) thinks the member from Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) is not justified in bringing before this House, what he regards as a grievance suffered by his constituents. The fact that parliament has taken no action in regard to any particular matter that an hon. member may think is deserving of consideration, is no reason, whatever why he should not take every reasonable occasion to bring it before parliament and the government.

All that my hon. friend (Mr. Henderson) said was, that if these are good claims they ought to have been brought to the attention of the House before this late date. That seems to me a very substantial point, and it has not been answered by the minister. If they have been brought to the attention of the government, then the censure which my hon. friend from Halton attributes to the two hon. gentlemen, is simply transferred to the government which has not dealt with claims which are alleged to be just, and which have remained unsettled for the eight years that my hon. friend from Saskatchewan has bten sitting in the House.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hou. friend (Mr. Davis) has brought these claims more than once to the attention of the House, at all events he has brought them to the attention of the government. Whether the claims are good or not, the great difficulty which the government finds, is

in opening up this matter after such a lapse of time, and in view of the fact that a commission appointed by the late government passed upon them. Whether the decision of the commission was right or wrong, my friends on the other side will, I think, agree that it is very difficult to open such a case. That is the difficulty we have on our minds yet, and I am sorry to say the government has not been able to solve it. There is no objection to bring down 'the papers.

If the facts are as represented by the member for Saskatchewan-I am not here to say whether they are or not-and if this matter has been laid before the government on more than one occasion, then the government should have come to some conclusion before the lapse of eight years. I was under the impression that the hon. member for Saskatchewan was merely making a speech for (he coming election ; and considering that he is going to have a very hard fight, I thought that the House might be indulgent and give him an hour or two, although I would have thought that it would have been more courteous and more courageous if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Davis) had met his opponent face to face and had not availed of all the privileges which surround him in this House, for the purpose of attacking a man who is 2,000 miles away.

It would appear that a certain class of people had their claims paid liberally while another class of people whose claims were as just and honest, as proven under oath, were not compensated. If that be the case, then the government might inquire into tile matter even at this late date, and see that justice is done. It is not a matter between the member for Saskatchewan and the candidate that may run against him ; it is a matter that concerns the people of all Canada, and if the facts are as stated, it is never too late to render justice. I think myself, that the government would be justified in appointing an independent commission, the members of which would not be influenced by local considerations, to inquire into the case. If that be done,
I think it will be found that there are a rumber of people up there who. have been ili treated.

When I brought this question up in the House last year, the leader of the opposition claimed that he had not time to look into it. This session, the notice has been on the paper for six weeks, and if hon. gentlemen opposite cared anything about it, they could have got the papers and inquired into the matter. The hon. member (Mr. Pope) says I made an election speech, but surely I did not make an election speech two years ago and three years ago wuen I brought the matter up before.

Whenever I did bring it up, the gentlemen ot the opposition seemed to be dissatisfied. I bring the matter before parliament because the people whom I represent have requested me to do so. The hon. gentleman from Compton (Mr. Pope) thinks I am going to have a hard time to get elected. He need not trouble himself about that. If he can carry his county as easily as I can carry mine, he will be all right. He says I should not speak about a gentleman who is a thousand miles away, but 1 can tell him that X am not afraid to meet any one on the platform, and that I discussed this question before my constituents, but my opponent was never present although lie was invited to come. Right in his own town he was invited to discuss this question at a meeting, and the Conservative committee of Prince Albert sent a team out for him and he refused to come. The same thing occurred at Lindsay, and he would not face the music. There was a meeting at a place called Melfort where they were all American settlers, who perhaps never heard of the rebellion and who had no claims, and he wanted to discuss the rebellion claims there, but the people said they wanted live issues and would not listen to him. I told him at that meeting that X would call a meeting at Prince Albert the night before the election to discuss the matter, but he took good care that he was not present. The people did not kno -v then that he was pocketing $20 a day or they would have asked some question about it. I can tell the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pope) that 1 am not afraid to bring this matter up either here or anywhere else.
The last time I brought the matter up in this House I did not mention his name at all. Hon. gentlemen opposite asked for his name to-night, or I would not have mentioned it. How could I have made the case of these people plain ? Thousands of them signed petitions stating that this man had acted as a partisan, and asking for an investigation Into the facts of the case. I think it only right that that should be done, and I am glad to see that my hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Ross) has taken that ground. It is never too late to remedy a grievance and to see that justice is done to any portion of the community. These people, rightly or wrongly, say they have a grievance. They say : We have not been treated properly, while certain other people have been paid more than they should have been for political reasons. All they ask is that a commission be appointed to look into the matter and see whether their statements are correct or not. ' I do not think it is necessary to appoint an expensive commission. Why did not hon. gentlemen opposite when in power pay the claim of Mr. McLean? The late Minister of the Interior said he was entitled to be paid; Sir Donald A. Smith, Mr. Scarth, Mr. A. W. Ross, the present attorney general of Manitoba, the Hon.

Campbell, Mr. G. H. McDowell, the member for Saskatchewan at that time, Senator Schultz, Mr. Adam Brown, -who sat in this House for many years; all said it was an honest claim. It therefore comes with very bad grace from hon. gentlemen opposite to accuse him of not bringing up the matter before, though he had the chance time and again. I hope the government will look into the grievances of these people, and render justice to whom justice is due.

Mr. Speaker, it is very evident that the hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) is losing his influence with the party in pow'er. When our party was in power we were in the habit of pressing our claims on the ministers or in caucus. We used to go before our ministers and take with us our friends, the members who came from the same part of the country, and press our claims ; and if we were not able to induce the ministers to recognize our claims, we never had any chance in the House. The Liberals frequently said of the late lamented Nicholas Flood Davin that very often when addressing the House he was playing to the gallery in order that he might get something into his newspaper the next day. Of course, we would not accuse the hon. gentlemen, some of whom are newspaper proprietors and who have been taking up so much of the time of the House in discussing this matter of having any such object in view. All I can say is that these gentlemen have not that influence with their ministers which they ought to have or which we used to have with our ministers when we were on the other side of the House. My hon. friend from Victoria says that this matter should be looked into. Was there not a commission appointed at that time to look into it? I was not then in the House, but I believe there was a very important and upright commission appointed, at the head of which was Judge Street.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Not that commission. Judge Street was on the commission appointed in 1885, at the time of the rebellion, to consider the claims of the halfbreeds. I think Mr. McKay was the commissioner to look into these claims.
Mr. McKay and Judge Ouimet.

Well, that commission was appointed, and its report was laid before the House, and the government acted upon it. The statements made by the hon. member for Saskatchewan here to-day are largely matters of opinion, not matters of fact. He has stated these things as his opinion and the opinion of some other people who hold the same political views as he does. So that I do not believe he has any evidence that the commission entrusted with that very important mission was false to its duty ; and until evidence of that kind is Jaid before this House to show that that was the case, I think we should be spared any further trouble in the matter. My hon. friend says the gov-'

eminent must take that view, because they do not act. If they do not act, they evidently have not that confidence in the gentlemen who have brought this matter before the House that our government had in us in the days when we were on the other side of the House.
Motion agreed to.

(Translation) moved
For copies of all Orders in Council, documents, correspondence exchanged between the government, or any of the ministers, and any persons, regarding the Indian Reserve established by 14 and 15 Victoria, Chapter 106, in favour of the Iroquois Indians of Sault St. Louis and of the Lake of Two Mountains, and the exchange of that reserve for any other one or for any sum of money in favour of the same said Indians.
Mr. Speaker, in connection with this motion which appears on to-day's Order paper, I wish to make a few remarks with a view to obtaining from the government some explanation in regard thereto. I may say that this matter has helped a good deal in securing the return of my hon. friend the member for Terrebonne (Mr. Desjardins) at the recent by-election.
There has been for a good many years back, in the county of Terrebonne^ an Indian reserve known under the name of Doncaster. Last year the government caused a subsidy of $11,325 to be voted for the purpose of settling these claims and the right hon. Prime Minister gave the following particulars on page 13779 of Hansard :
To provide an amount for squatters' improvements, Doncaster reserve, $11,325.
I notice that in this year's estimates the above amount no longer appears, although as yet nothing has been paid on last j'ear's appropriation. However, the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Prefontaine), whenever an opportunity offers of meeting his political friends, and among others, those gentlemen whose names appear on page 13780 of ' Hansard-,' never fails to promise that their claims will be settled, notwithstanding the fact that the House has not been called upon to revote the subsidy granted last year.
Although the government have found out that the said amount cannot be paid, the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries still persists, as well as the Dominion and local members for Terrebonne, in promising to the electors of that part of the county that the government will grant them compensation for the improvements effected on the Indian reserve.
It is a matter of surprise, Mr. Speaker, that the government, through one of its leading members, the Minister of Marine, should have agreed to compensate people who had illegally set foot on a reserve, for fifty years

back the property of the Oka and Caughna-waga Iroquois.
Last year, as may be seen by referring to page 13779 of * Hansard,' the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) asked for some explanations in reference to these $11,325, and the right hon. Prime Minister replied that the amount was voted to compensate the following persons : Israel Thouin, $3,000; Isidore Legault, $800; Napoleon Constantineau, $540. The right hon. gentleman did not condescend to give the names of the recipients of the balance of the $11,000 ; but I believe I am right when I say that the other recipients were the leading party heelers of the hon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Desjardins) during the recent by-elec-tion.
The government would be willing to compensate people who have no right to any compensation, who have ignored the law, who, in spite of their knowledge of the circumstances of the case, that is, although they knew that those lands belonged to Indians, settled on them. I hope that this year, the right hon. gentleman will take this opportunity to give further explanations. He, no doubt, has realized that the government have no right to pay the amount voted last year, and that is the reason why it was cut out of the estimates now laid before the House.
I have raised this question, in order to put a stop to reports circulated in the county of Terrebonne by the representatives of that county, both in the Dominion and local House, to the effect that the question has been settled by the government and that the gentlemen whose names have been given by the right hon. Prime Minister are to be compensated! for improvements which they should not have effected, aud are to receive amounts to which they are not entitled, in connection with an expenditure controlled by nobody and authorized by nobody. As a matter of fact the only title these people have in the minds of the government is the fact that they have been devoted supporters of the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Prefontaine) when he was a candidate in that county, and also that they have been zealous supporters of the hon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Dejardins) and of Mr. Prevost, the local member.
I would like to have full and precise particulars as to this matter from the right hon. Prime Minister, who, I believe was wrongly informed when he gave to the House the answer to be found on page 13779 of ' Hansard,' for 1903. I do not intend to read just now what he said at the time; but those desirous of perusing it have only to refer to the page quoted above.
In the county of my hon. friend from Terrebonne, that matter in connection with the Indian reserve is a burning one, and has been so for over twenty years past

It has not been found possible to settle the question heretofore, as the Indians of the township of Doncaster are the actual and sole proprietors of that reserve; they are in full possession of lands granted to them under 14 Victoria, August 30, 1851. If my information is correct, the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries stated in the county of Terrebonne, at several public meetings at which he was called upon to speak, that the matter would be settled, and would be settled by himself and his government.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. PREFONTAINE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries).
speechtext: (Translation.) Certainly.

(Translation.) The hon. minister says : Certainly. I am very happy indeed that the matter should be settled at last, and that the electors of Terrebonne whom he has converted to his views by such promises should at last be satisfied.
I therefore submit this proposition, seconded by my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), and hope that not only will the government bring down the papers for which I ask, but that the right hon. Prime Minister will gladly take this opportunity to give explanations which will satisfy the members of this House and the electors of the province of Quebec, as the latter, relying on those given during last session, had gathered the idea that this matter of interest to part of the inhabitants of the country north of Montreal would be finally settled.
(Translation.) Is the hon. member for Laval agreeable or not to a settlement being effected ?

(Translation.) Will the right hon. gentleman allow me to ask him
: Does he think the squatters are entitled to compensation ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Certainly.
(Translation.)
(Translation.) On what grounds ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
(Translation.) On grounds of natural equity. My hon. friend is well aware that the public lands m the province of Quebec are open" to settlement, and it is hard to decide that a settler who takes up land in some township or other acting in good faith, believing that the land belongs to the Crown, shall be deprived of it without compensation. As those who settled up there were in good faith, we deemed it proper to compensate them for the losses they had sustained.
If I understood him rightly, my hon. friend is in favour of a settlement being effected by the government. He has just stated to the hon. Minister of Marine that he is in favour of a settlement being effected ; he wanted the settlers to be compensated.
(Translation.) I am-in favour of compensating those who are entitled to such compensation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: (Translation.) Who are those entitled to compensation ? As for us, we believe that all those who have settled there are entitled to compensation. And that "was also the opinion of parliament last year when they voted the necessary funds for that purpose. The only reason why those moneys were not paid was the necessity of finding out the exact status of those for whom we sought compensation. But as soon as satisfactory reports have been received, the settlers will be paid.

(Translation.) If, in accordance with the hope expressed by the hon. Prime Minister, the government pays those claims before the end of the current year, and if the settlement is effected on a fair basis, the motion of my hon. friend from Laval (Mr. Leonard) will have had, to say the least, the effect of bringing about the settlement of these claims more promptly than would have happened otherwise.

Now, a rather strange circumstance, anil worthy of attention, is that, although this amount has been due for a good many months past, nothing has been done towards paying it. Nevertheless, according to the right hon. gentleman, the -money was due at the time the vote was granted. At all events, X think this motion will have been of actual service to these claimants.	_
In this connection there are two theories current; it is difficult to say which is true. The reserve in question was granted to the Indians over fifty years ago. The right hon. gentleman stated that people had settled on the reserve without knowing that it belonged to the Indians, and had made improvements on it. These settlers having afterwards applied to the provincial government for a title were told that they could not get it.
That is why, according to the Prime Minister considerable time had elapsed. The claimants then applied to the Dominion government and the latter, to settle the question, thought fit to have recourse to compensation, while at the same time seeking to induce the Indians to relinquish their title to the reserve which had been granted to them fiftv years ago. In the meantime, however, improvements had been effected by these settlers and it had become necessary to compensate them. That is the explanation given in last year's ' Hansard ' in regard to the item of $11,325.	.
If these claims be clear and precise, why have they not been settled before this ? That is what, no doubt, will be shown by the correspondence to be brought down in compliance with this motion.
But there is another theory which I heard in the county of Terrebonne, in several places and on various occasions, and it is to the effect that these people had settled there knowing perfectly well what were the rights of these Indians.
(Translation.) How could they know ?
(Translation.) Very easily, since this reserve was granted over fifty years ago.
(Translation.) But they might not have been aware of it.

(Translation.) The fact of that grant having been made to the Indians was known to all. If the improvements referred to were effected in good faith, the matter might be considered ; but if, as was reported to me, these improvements have been carried out on the assurances given by my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, it is quite a different matter.
(Translation.) In 1896, when I went there for the first time, I was not even aware that these people were settled on that reserve.

Pledges have been given in connection with the settlement of this question of the Doncaster Indian reserve, notwithstanding which it is not yet settled. The amount has been voted for a long time back, and if the theory referred to is correct, that is if these people have settled there knowing quite well what difficulties they would have to overcome to secure a title, then I maintain that the moneys voted might be better employed elsewhere. Thus, in the city of Montreal, there are some very urgent needs which should be attended to before complying with the demands of these claimants. The post office people are requesting fairer treatment, and are being told that money cannot be found to meet their requirements. If the report as to the origin of these claims is correct, this amount would be better expended in meeting such reasonable claims as those I have just referred to, instead of these others which are, to say the least, ot very doubtful character. I think the motion wili have the effect of hastening the settlement of the question ; and if the claims are legitimate they shall be paid as they should in justice be.
iMr. PREFONT AINE. (Translation). It is clear from the remarks just made by the hon. members for Laval and Jacques Cartier, that they are not at all agreeable to a settlement of these claims; because, if they were agreeable to such a settlement, what would be the sense of questioning the rights of these settlers, and especially of questioning them with such persistency 1 From what the hon. member for Jacques Cartier has said, it is clear that the government are taken to task for having undertaken to deal with that question and to bring about a settlement, while these gentlemen on the other side had never bothered their heads with it, had looked down upon it as ridiculous,-and that to my personal knowledge,-adding that public interest required that the question should be discarded. Well, very likely it is through mere spite that they now rebuke the government for having kept their pledge.
I am familiar with the circumstances in all their particulars. The Indian reserve of Doncaster was granted in 1850 or 1851. A considerable area had been set apart for the Indians, who, however, never took possession until twelve or eighteen months ago, when they heard of negotiations being carried on through the Department of the Interior with a view of settling the matter. Thet first proposal which was made to the Indians concerned was that they should relinquish for a consideration, the rights they might have on the lands occupied by the squatters. I have not seen the report of the surveyor instructed to mark the limits of the townships-and that is one reason why the settlement has been deferred-but I understand that the church of Ste. Lucie is situated on the Indian reserve. Now, in

the interest of the poor settlers of that parish, it was important that the question should be settled.
Negotiations were carried on for a period of two- years between the department of the Interior and the Indians. I know that at one time, some Indians went to the reserve and by sheer force took possession of the improvements effected by the settlers. So, there was only one thing to do, since the Indians-unfairly to my mind-would not relinquish their rights, and that was to decide whether it was just to expel these squatters without compensation. The matter was carefully looked into by the Department of the Interior, and after a thorough investigation the conclusion was that the settlers had acted in good faith. There is no sense in saying that some of these settlers took up land with a view to securing compensation from the government. I am conversant with the facts, and I may state that none of these settlers took up land there with such an object in view. The later arrivals have been settled there for at least ten years and the others for twenty-five or thirty years.
Now, the good faith of these settlers is proven by the facts ; that reserve, which was established by statute, had no limits whatever marked out. It was stated that an Indian reserve had been set apart there, but, with the leave of the provincial government, it had been laid bare of all its timber of commercial value ; lumbering had been carried on for several years on these lands, and it was quite natural that people without much education, and not conversant with the law, should have thought that they were settling on the public domain, and not on an Indian reserve.
The charge that I suggested to these people to settle on that reserve is so preposterous, so childish, that I do not think it is necessary to answer it. These settlers who had been hobnobbed by the conservative government, saw fit to change their political allegiance m 1900 ; but that is quite easy to understand. Instead of telling these people as did the conservative government : You aie not bona fide settlers, you have no right to any compensation ; we told them that we acknowledged their rights and that we would endeavour to settle the question in a fair ancl satisfactory way.
That is a very important matter, not only for the parish of Ste. Lucie, but for the *w hole of the counties of Montcalm and Terrebonne. We said that if it were possible to induce the Indians to give up the reserve and to settle on other lands which the government would provide, so much the better tor those two counties and for the squatters concerned. That is all there is to it ; and it seems to me nothing unusual has occurred under the circumstances.
Such was the good faith of these- settlers, that they offered to pay to the government the same price for these lands as"that asked
for Crown lands. They claim fair treatment only, and it is unfortunate that these poor squatters should have been deprived of the benefit of that settlement until to-day.
I should say in passing that the amount voted last year in favour of these settlers includes the cost of opening a road connecting the two counties of Terrebonne and Montcalm and crossing' this reserve. If the settlement of the m'atter has been deferred, there is good reason for it : it was necessary to "find out exactly whether the squatters who had taken up lands there were on lots included in the reserve, or on Crown lands under the control of the Quebec government. That is why the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) came to an undestanding with the Quebec government on that subject, whereupon the latter instructed one of their officials to mark out the exact limits of Doncaster. The report of that gentleman has been handed to the department two or three weeks ago, and the official entrusted with that task is busy just now settling the matter in a way satisfactory to all concerned.
I was surprised to hear the member for Laval cast blame right and left, after stating that he was in favour of a settlement being-effected, and charge the Minister of Marine and Fisheries with having suggested to tnose people to take up lands on that reserve. I may state to the hon. member that the 'information supplied to him is altogether incorrect. Never did I make such a suggestion. What we stated in the county of Terrebonne, we are ready to repeat here and elsewhere. We ascertained that this was a case of hardship, and the government did not hesitate in doing justice. We requested that fait treatment be extended to these poor settlers, and if we did wrong in making such a request, we are willing to abide by the consequences ; but I may say that we are ready to take the same position to-morrow, should circumstances warrant us in doing so, as the correspondence will show they did warrant us in this case. ,

(Translation.) Will the hon. minister allow me to put one question: if, last yjar, the government did not know what were the limits of the township of Doncaster, why did they ask for a vote of $11,300 ?

(Translation.) Before the sale of cheese was taken up, M.
K. Everetts, the extensive cheese manufacturer, who now resides in Smith's Falls, spoke at considerable length, roundly denouncing the Ottawa government on its dairy policy, particularly the introduction of the experimental cheese curing stations which he characterized as the biggest humbug ever imposed upon the people. Mr. Everetts introduced the subject by reference to the resolution from the Ottawa Cheese Board, read at a pervious meeting of th Brockville Cheese Board, asking the co-operation of the latter organization in bringing before the Eastern Ontario Butter and Cheese Association the matter of having cheese graded as finest, seconds and thirds. He did not agree with the suggestion. Brockville section was making nothing but finests and he urged the Brockville board to have nothing to do with the scheme whatever. This led up to a fierec attack upon the methods adopted by Prof. Ruddick, chief of the dairy division, in the discharge of his duties. Mr. Everetts took occasion to hand out a few caustic remarks bearing on the government curing stations, one of which is established in Brockville. The Ottawa government, he held, in creating these stations, was taking upon itself a burden which the calls of the trade did not demand. Each province should look after its own improved methods of manufacture, while the duty of the Dominion government was to provide for up-to-date transportation services by rail and water. The money used in the erection and carrying on of these curing rooms was a useless expenditure. Mr. Everetts' claimed that the results achieved did not warrant their continuance in operation. They did not aid the patrons in obtaining one-sixteenth of a cent more for their cheese than others. He challenged a single person to contradict him. These rooms were held up as models for others to follow. How many had built curing rooms after the fashion of the Brockville ' pine monument.' Not a one. And as to the cost of construction, operation, &c., the country was yet in darkness, notwithstanding a deliberate promise made by Prof. Ruddick last year to give such information. ed that at the gatherings of * experts' to talk over matters pertaining to the trade, manufacturers and producers-the big men behind the industry, the men who have invested their money-were not called in consultation.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
It was at the meeting held last fall at Broefcville. Tlie government were establishing a station there, and strongly advised the farmers to draw their cheese and put it in storage there, and have it undergo this curing process by cold storage or whatever process the hon. minister may call it. rlhis was the plan adopted in the cheese establishment there. If a man came with a load of cheese, they would take one cheese out and weigh it and put it upstairs in the curing room and would weigh the- other and putting it down in the cold storage. If the one they put in the curing room upstairs shrank two or five pounds more than the one downstairs, they charged what the shrinkage was for the handling of the man's cheese. As they could not get the farmers to bring in their cheese, the government hired an army of officials to go through the country and drum up men to draw the cheese in, and large sums were paid to people last year to bring in cheese to the Brockville curing cooling station. As much as $1,011 was paid for this purpose * and the farmers tell me that the room which the government have to experiment in upstairs is not at all in touch with the curing rooms the farmers have throughout their factories in the country. They have a pretty hot sweating room so as to make the cheese as light as they can and charge so much a pound for the shrinkage. The cheese they put downstairs of course retains its weight. The government have also developed another fad. They covered the cheese with a kind of wax called paraffin. Last year they paid for paraffin wax 1.2C3 pounds at 7 cents ; 1.045 at 7J and 1.070 at Si. What effect has this paraffin on the cheese in the market of England ? Let me read a clipping taken from the ' Trade Bulletin ' a few days ago. written by its special correspondent in London :
^ The London special correspondent of the 'Trade Bulletin' writes that journal : 'Bristol buyers advise me this week that there is too much waxed cheese coming in, and as they have objected to this before, it is a pity makers do not take the hint.'
The ' Trade Bulletin ' thereupon returns to the discussion of the subject and says : ' It is-to be regretted that the government Agricultural Department at Ottawa should have advocated the waxing of cheese with paraffine by faetorymen, especially as there is such great objection to paraffined cheese on the other side of the Atlantic, and as our makers are supposed to study the requirements of the trade there, it is to be hoped that they will discontinue this highly objectionable practice. A Montreal exporter while in England last fall was instructed by three firms there not to ship them a box. of waxed cheese, as their customers strongly objected to them, on the ground that the goods lost considerable in weight, one importer stating that he w-ould not buy waxed cheese unless he was allowed two pounds per box. What is required in the English market is cheese with a.bright natural skin in the summer time, and cheese made in the fall should appear in the natural condition with a nice dry and green mold on the skin, showing a little maturity. Paraffined cheese prevents this natural appearance, besides causing loss in weight to the retailer. As so many objections continue to be raised, in the great consuming centres of Great Britain against waxing cheese, surely our faetorymen will not persist in a practice that is calculated to injure the enviable prestige of their goods in the English market.'
The hon. gentleman not only put the country to an expense of perhaps $100,000 in building and equipping these four cheesecuring stations, but he advocated the paraffining of the cheese, so as to prevent them, as it as said, from losing weight and causing them to command a higher price in the English market. And what is the effect ? Our cheese is selling at from three cents to five cents per pound less than it sold for a year ago. And this is largely due to the Minister of Agriculture advocating the paraffining of the cheese. We have lost standing in the English market. I do not know what the hon. Minister of Agriculture will have to say in answer to his political friend Mr. Everetts, of Brockville, who charges him, more strongly than I can state it, with responsibility for this condition of affairs. He says that men in high places are playing to the gallery and making use of fads to the injury of the cheese industry which the people of this country built up before the hon. gentleman became minister. And the hon. minister is trying to make people think that he is doing something for them by establishing these illustration stations for the factory men to occupy, though they have the cooling stations that are superior to those the hon. gentleman has established. And none of these practical men favour this fad, whether of the minister or of the commissioner, of paraffining cheese to prevent them from losing in weight. Englishmen do not want that and so our cheese are practically set aside. The hon. gentleman will understand that is not my statement that he has to answer, but that of Mr. Everetts. Every one who knows that gentleman knows that, from boyhood, he has been one of the strongest Reformers in the country. And he knows what he is talking about in discussing dairying questions. He runs eighteen or twenty factories of his own and is a purchaser of cheese in the Brockville district. The loss at the Brockville station is small as compared with

that of Woodstock. It is $2,255 at Brockville, while it is $9,864 at Woodstock. In Brockville, the cheese purchased and cured was $4,497.96 and the hauling cost $1,011.60. The details of these expenditures can be found at page D-100 of the Auditor General's Report. The accounts show that the amounts paid out for cheese purchased and hauled for Brockville, Cowansville, Woodstock and St. Hyacinthe was $20,828.20. The proceeds from the sales of cheese amounted to $15,810.55. But the Auditor General puts in a remark to this effect:
Proceeds from sales of cheese (receipts from cheese paid for In June and July, 1903 (1902-3), not in this account, payments in above).
So, we do not know what that amount was, and we cannot say what the profit or loss was on the purchase and hauling of this cheese. That is why we want a detailed account. Prof. Ruddick has promised it for the last year or two to the Brockville men, and they cannot get it- so Mr. Everetts states. They want to know how much the station is costing and how much the loss has been. They want it in the interest of cheese producers of that section, to show what this fad-whether it is the Minister's or Prof. Robertson's, they do not know-is resulting. At any rate, they say that as cheese producers they do not want it, but that it is money thrown away. I bring the matter to the attention of the House and the country that we may have an opportunity to hear what answer the minister will give to the charge made by Mr. Everetts.

I can assure him that the information is too voluminous to be given in answer to a question. I told him before that I would facilitate the return, and I can assure him now' that he shall have it in a short time. As to the remarks of the hon. gentleman,
I wTill say only a few words. I have not the full information before me. When the facts are before the House I am sure the hon. gentleman will have an opportunity of discussing them to his full content. The statements he has made in regard to the Brockville factory are not quite correct so far as the spirit and intention of them is concerned. The plan of establishing a central cool curing room for cheese was one that was discussed in the various association meetings for twro years-proposed to the people who are interested in dairying and discussed thoroughly. The reason for this proposition was that for some time, (here had been considerable complaints concerning lack of uniformity in the quality of our cheese put on the English market. We had been warned over and over again . by those handling Canadian cheese in the English market that the curing of our cheese was not satisfactory. The investigation showed very clearly that the unsatisfactory curing of our cheese was due to the very changeable temperature in the curing rooms of the various factories throughout the country-not merely different temperature in different rooms, but great changes of temperature in the same room, often within twenty-four hours, the curing rooms being so constructed that the managers of factories could not control the temperature in them. It is wrell known and understood that the home-made cheese in England commanded higher prices than ours; and experts who examined them and compared them carefully with our cheese in England found certain difficulties which were well recognized and which caused a higher price to be given for English and Scotch cheese. The reason was found to be that in the curing rooms in the English cheese factories, the temperature was actually under control. They were so well constructed that the managers could keep the temperature at an even level of from 60 to 65 degrees, while, in me curing rooms of the Canadian factories, the temperature frequently went down to 50 degrees or so at night and would rise to 75 or 80 degrees in the heat of the day. The proposition was put before the dairymen and '.bey asked that the department should undertake experiments in this line. The questions how the experiments should be carried on, and on what scale they should be carried on wrere carefully considered. It was felt to be necessary that these experiments should be carried on on such a -scale that there would be a sufficient amount of cheese cured to secure a fair expression

of opinion from the buyers in England as well as from the handlers of this country. Therefore, it was necessary to provide curing rooms which would handle a very large quantity of cheese. We picked out four dairy districts, two in the province of Ontario and two in the province of Quebec, and asked the farmers, through the cheese factory men, to send in their cheese to be cured in these thoroughly equipped and well constructed curing rooms.
Two of them, that at Cowansville and that at Woodstock, were equipped with mechanical cold storage, and those at Brockville and St. Hyaeinthe were equipped with ice coll storage, in order to see whether the one *which is much more economical than the other can be satisfactorily managed and carried out. The work was experimental in its character, and therefore required, nor simply attention to the work of curing the *cheese, but o;f careful observation and watching and careful comparison, as my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) has mentioned by the curing of some cheese under ordinal'} conditions and by the curing of others in well constructed curing rooms. This work has been managed successfully, if I may say so, notwithstanding what the hon. gen tleman has said and read. It has been so successful that this last season we had applications for three or four times as much cheese as the room could accommodate. The first year there was some doubt and suspicion. The people who owned factories in the neighbourhood of St. Hyaeinthe, Brockville Cowansville and Woodstock did not know what the results would be, and were a little doubtful about what might occur. It was an experiment (and they did not know. But those who had sent in their cheese were so eminently satisfied with the results in the line of the shrinkage of their cheese and in the better prices which they obtained, that we had applications to take more cheese than our buildings would accommodate. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) says that Mr. Everetts declared it was not successful. I have no report of the meeting where Mr. Everetts made that suggestion ; I do not know his opinion on the matter, but I can read to the House, and perhaps will have an opportunity of doing so before the House prorogues, dozens of statements from leading cheese-makers, buyers of cheese and buyers of cheese in England, that cheese cured at these factories was far superior to the average Canadian cheese, that the experiment was an absolute success, and that the desire was expressed that all Canadian cheese might be cured under such conditions, and sent forward of the quality of that cured in these cheese rooms. I did not know that the hon. gentleman was going to bring this matter up to-night, and have not these statements of those in the trade and the resolutions passed by various dairy associations, produce associations and others who have closely watched results.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: When the hon. gentleman's estimates come up we will be glad to discuss it.

I will be very glad to discuss it then. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) has spoken of the expense, and has taken the figures from the Auditor General's Report. These figures do not show the profits on the curing of the cheese ; they simply show the expenditure in the experimental work and the actual sales of certain cheese. There were thousands and thousands of boxes of cheese that passed through these factories the profits on which do not appear, because they went to the factorymen who owned the cheese. This cheese was handled for these factorymen by the government, and the factorymen reaped the benefit. The government only reaped the benefit of the satisfaction which these factorymen whose cheese went to these curing rooms have abundantly expressed. The department has the satisfaction of knowing what can be done in cool curing rooms. The results are for the benefit of the dairying interests of this country, and, having proved that, we are well content to rest our reputation and the future on the proof which is given, not to the hon. gentleman, but to the dairymen of Canada, who will abundantly support the action of the department.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What about the paraffining of cheese ?

An experiment was also made in the paraffining of cheese. A large number were paraffined and some were not. When the paraffined cheese was first sent over to England the English market, not knowing what they were and what the result might be, expressed a little dissatisfaction and doubt, but since that time we have abundant reports from the English buyers of paraffined cheese, that the experiment is successful, that the cheese so treated have turned out exceedingly well in the English market, that the cheese so treated have shrunk less and have given a better result to the people who have sent them forward than other cheese.
